title: 嘉靖八年會試錄
text:
會試錄序
我
皇上承統御宇明物察倫以為民
極以昭
文明之治其盛矣乎歲己丑復
當會試天下士禮部尚書臣
方獻夫侍郎臣李時臣嚴嵩
===
以
舊制請天下之士莫不奮然興裒
然集咸有帝臣之願焉詩曰
豈弟君子遐不作人其斯之
謂與先是臣竊念
國家用人以科舉為重而有司
選士以鄉舉為先因條三事

===
以
舊制請天下之士莫不奮然興衰
然集咸有帝臣之願焉詩曰
豈弟君子遐不作人其斯之
謂與先是臣竊念
國家用人以科舉為重而有司
選士以鄉舉為先因條三事
punctuated:
會試錄序

我皇上承統御宇，明物察倫，以為民極，以昭文明之治，其盛矣乎！歲己丑，復當會試天下士，禮部尚書臣方獻夫、侍郎臣李時、臣嚴嵩，以舊制請。天下之士莫不奮然興、裒然集，咸有帝臣之願焉。《詩》曰：「豈弟君子，遐不作人。」其斯之謂與！先是，臣竊念國家用人以科舉為重，而有司選士以鄉舉為先，因條三事
translation_en:
Preface to the Metropolitan Examination Record

Our Emperor has succeeded to the imperial line and rules the realm, discerning the nature of things and examining human relationships, thereby serving as the people's supreme standard and manifesting enlightened governance. How flourishing it is! In the year jichou [1529], the time again came to hold the Metropolitan Examination for scholars from throughout the realm. Your servants Fang Xianfu, Minister of Rites, and Li Shi and Yan Song, Vice Ministers, requested its convening in accordance with established regulations. Scholars throughout the realm rose eagerly and gathered in great numbers, all aspiring to become servants of the Emperor. The Book of Odes says: “The gracious and kindly lord—does he not nurture men?” Surely this describes the present occasion! Before this, your servant had privately reflected that the state places great weight on the civil-service examinations in recruiting men, while the responsible officials begin the selection of scholars with the Provincial Examination. I therefore set out three matters…

title: 嘉靖八年會試錄
text:
上請一曰正文體二曰明實錄三
曰慎考官
上俞之既令行天下矣及是禮部
以甲科取士所關尤重復申
明三事以
請
上復俞之俾昭示焉然不以臣為
===
愚
命主試事臣受
命夙夜不遑夫文體不正則實錄
難明考官不慎則文體難正
皇上慎重之託濫及愚臣其何能
勝諸謹率同事矢心秉公合
天下之士如

translation_en: …submitted a petition to the throne: first, to rectify literary style; second, to make the records accurate and clear; third, to exercise care in choosing Examiners. His Majesty approved these proposals, and orders had already been issued to implement them throughout the realm. At this juncture, the Ministry of Rites, considering that selecting men through the higher examination involved matters of particular importance, again set forth these three proposals in a petition. His Majesty again approved them and ordered that they be publicly proclaimed. Yet he did not deem your servant too foolish, and commanded me to preside over the examination. Having received this command, I had no respite, morning or night. For unless literary style is rectified, it is difficult to make the records accurate and clear; unless Examiners are carefully chosen, it is difficult to rectify literary style. His Majesty’s weighty trust has undeservedly fallen upon your foolish servant: how could I be equal to it? With due reverence, I led my colleagues in pledging ourselves to impartiality and assembled the scholars of the realm, in accordance with…

title: 嘉靖八年會試錄
text:
制而三試之觀經義之文多發
明理致不事浮夸知初試之
變也觀詔誥表論判之文多
率循典實不事奇怪知再試
之變也觀五策之文多經略
世故不事剽竊知三試之變
也臣乃稽首颺言曰我
===
皇上神化之速一至是乎諸士子
之文可謂善變矣可采錄矣
臣等司考校者可無慮矣語
曰文莫吾猶人也躬行君子
則吾未之有得大聖人猶自
責實如此今
國家以文取士豈非因之而責

===
皇上神化之速一至是乎諸士子
之文可謂善變矣可采錄矣
臣等司考校者可無慮矣語
曰文莫吾猶人也躬行君子
則吾未之有得大聖人猶自
責實如此今
國家以文取士豈非因之而責
punctuated:
制而三試之。觀經義之文，多發明理致，不事浮夸，知初試之變也；觀詔誥表論判之文，多率循典實，不事奇怪，知再試之變也；觀五策之文，多經略世故，不事剽竊，知三試之變也。臣乃稽首颺言曰：「我皇上神化之速，一至是乎！諸士子之文，可謂善變矣，可采錄矣！臣等司考校者，可無慮矣！」
語曰：「文，莫吾猶人也；躬行君子，則吾未之有得。」大聖人猶自責實如此。今國家以文取士，豈非因之而責
translation_en:
…in accordance with the regulations, and examined them in three sessions. On inspecting their essays on the meaning of the Classics, I found that many elucidated principles and their implications, without indulging in empty embellishment: this showed the change in the first session. On inspecting their edicts, proclamations, memorials, discourses, and legal judgments, I found that many adhered to established models and substantive content, without pursuing the bizarre: this showed the change in the second session. On inspecting their five policy essays, I found that many addressed the management of worldly affairs, without resorting to plagiarism: this showed the change in the third session. Your servant then bowed his head to the ground and proclaimed: “Has the swiftness of our Emperor’s wondrous transforming influence reached such a height! The candidates’ writings may indeed be said to have changed for the better and to merit selection for inclusion in this record. We servants charged with examining and assessing them may now be free from anxiety!”
The Analects says: “In literary learning, perhaps I am the equal of others; but as for putting the conduct of a gentleman into practice, I have not yet attained it.” Even the great sage held himself accountable for actual practice in this way. Now that the state selects men through their writing, is it not thereby demanding of them…

title: 嘉靖八年會試錄
text:
其躬行之實矣乎夫自古聖
王之教皆所以明人倫也故
道德一風俗同而仁義之言
孝弟之行達之天下也肆我
皇上以孝治天下而德教加于百
姓刑于四海凡有得於觀感
者殆莫不興行而能言其實
===
况士自鄉而升為民之俊秀
者乎故凡為畔道背經之說
靡不懲創前非行修言道非
徒文體之正而已是之謂大
同則夫
今日人文之盛信有在於我
皇上鼓舞作興者矣記曰天下有

===
況士自鄉而升為民之俊秀
者乎故凡為畔道背經之說
靡不懲創前非行修言道非
徒文體之正而已是之謂大
同則夫
今日人文之盛信有在於我
皇上鼓舞作興者矣記曰天下有
punctuated: 其躬行之實矣乎？夫自古聖王之教，皆所以明人倫也。故道德一，風俗同，而仁義之言、孝弟之行達之天下也。肆我皇上以孝治天下，而德教加于百姓，刑于四海。凡有得於觀感者，殆莫不興行而能言其實，况士自鄉而升、為民之俊秀者乎？故凡為畔道背經之說，靡不懲創前非，行修言道，非徒文體之正而已。是之謂大同。則夫今日人文之盛，信有在於我皇上鼓舞作興者矣。《記》曰：「天下有
translation_en: …the substance of their conduct in practice? From antiquity, the teachings of sage kings have all served to clarify human relationships. Thus moral principles were unified and customs made concordant, while words of benevolence and righteousness and acts of filial piety and fraternal respect spread throughout the realm. Now Our Emperor governs all under Heaven through filial piety: his moral instruction reaches the common people and serves as a model throughout the Four Seas. Almost everyone who has learned from observing and being moved by his example has been stirred to act and can speak of what they have put into practice. How much more must this be true of the scholars who have advanced from their localities as the outstanding talents among the people? Thus all who have propounded views that depart from the Way and contravene the Classics have taken warning from their former errors, cultivated their conduct, and spoken in accordance with the Way. This is more than merely a rectification of literary style. This is what is called the Great Unity. The flourishing of literary culture today surely owes much to Our Emperor’s encouragement and inspiration. The Book of Rites says: “When all under Heaven possesses…”

title: 嘉靖八年會試錄
text:
道則行有枝葉天下無道則
辭有枝葉夫辭有枝葉虛文
也行有枝葉躬行之實也然
則我
祖宗設科以文取士端有在於斯
矣夫有實言者有實用善作
人者必得人舍是而虛文之
求抑末矣本之則無固非我
祖宗設科垂法之意亦非我
皇上神化作人之道也嗚呼敢不
慎諸敢不慎諸夫士凡三千
七百餘人取三百二十名遵
制額也敢謂能盡人之才乎哉
嗣此而益涵濡

punctuated: 道，則行有枝葉；天下無道，則辭有枝葉。」夫辭有枝葉，虛文也；行有枝葉，躬行之實也。然則我祖宗設科，以文取士，端有在於斯矣。夫有實言者有實用，善作人者必得人。舍是而虛文之求，抑末矣，本之則無，固非我祖宗設科垂法之意，亦非我皇上神化作人之道也。嗚呼！敢不慎諸？敢不慎諸？夫士凡三千七百餘人，取三百二十名，遵制額也。敢謂能盡人之才乎哉？嗣此而益涵濡
translation_en: …the Way prevails, conduct has branches and leaves; when the Way does not prevail in the world, words have branches and leaves.” Words having branches and leaves means empty literary embellishment; conduct having branches and leaves means the substance of personal practice. Thus, our imperial ancestors’ purpose in establishing the examinations and selecting men through their writing lay precisely here. Those whose words have substance possess practical usefulness; those skilled in nurturing talent will surely obtain worthy men. To abandon this and seek empty literary embellishment is to pursue mere externals, with nothing at the root. This assuredly accords neither with our imperial ancestors’ intention in establishing the examinations and handing down their regulations, nor with our Emperor’s way of nurturing talent through his wondrous transforming influence. Alas! Dare we fail to exercise care? Dare we fail to exercise care? There were over 3,700 candidates in all, of whom 320 were selected, in accordance with the prescribed quota. Could we venture to claim that we have fully encompassed everyone’s talents? Henceforth, may they be still more deeply imbued with…

title: 嘉靖八年會試錄
text:
聖化以儲世用其有艾乎哉是舉
也奉
詔命為考試官者大學士臣璁
學士臣韜也其同考試官則
右中允臣道南修撰臣以訓
臣用卿臣用賓右賛善臣文
俊臣昂編修臣教臣星臣衮
===
臣維傑臣璐都給事中臣臯
謨給事中臣鶴鳴臣準署郎
中臣儒署員外郎臣黙主事
臣禎也其監試官則御史臣
濂臣煦也暨諸執事厥責惟
均凡此同事之人既事之後
尚宜仰思我

punctuated: 聖化，以儲世用，其有艾乎哉？是舉也，奉詔命為考試官者，大學士臣璁、學士臣韜也。其同考試官則右中允臣道南，修撰臣以訓、臣用卿、臣用賓，右賛善臣文俊、臣昂，編修臣教、臣星、臣衮、臣維傑、臣璐，都給事中臣臯謨，給事中臣鶴鳴、臣準，署郎中臣儒，署員外郎臣黙，主事臣禎也。其監試官則御史臣濂、臣煦也。暨諸執事，厥責惟均。凡此同事之人，既事之後，尚宜仰思我
translation_en:
…the sage’s transforming influence, thereby preparing themselves for service to the age: could there ever be an end to this? For this examination, those appointed Examiners by imperial command were your servants Cong, Grand Secretary, and Tao, Academician.

The Associate Examiners were your servant Daonan, Right Companion of the Heir Apparent; your servants Yixun, Yongqing, and Yongbin, Senior Compilers; your servants Wenjun and Ang, Right Admonishers of the Heir Apparent; your servants Jiao, Xing, Gun, Weijie, and Lu, Junior Compilers; your servant Gaomo, Chief Supervising Secretary; your servants Heming and Zhun, Supervising Secretaries; your servant Ru, Acting Bureau Director; your servant Mo, Acting Vice Director; and your servant Zhen, Secretary.

title: 嘉靖八年會試錄
text:
皇上作人之功益勵實行以共承
休德為多士先焉錄成以
獻臣以職事忝序諸首
光祿大夫柱國少傅兼太
子太傅吏部尚書
謹身殿大學士張璁謹序
alt_text:
皇上作人之功益勵實行以共承
休德爲多士先焉録成以
獻臣以職事忝序諸首
光禄大夫柱國少傅兼　太
子太傅吏部尚書
謹身殿大學士張璁謹序
punctuated:
皇上作人之功，益勵實行，以共承休德，為多士先焉。錄成，以獻。臣以職事，忝序諸首。
光祿大夫、柱國、少傅兼太子太傅、吏部尚書、謹身殿大學士張璁謹序。
translation_en:
…His Majesty’s achievement in nurturing talent, and strive still harder in actual conduct, together upholding his illustrious virtue and setting an example for the many scholars. The record having been completed, it is presented to the throne. By virtue of my official duties, I, your servant, have presumed to place this preface at its beginning.
Respectfully prefaced by Zhang Cong 張璁, Grand Master for Splendid Happiness, Pillar of State, Junior Mentor concurrently Grand Tutor of the Heir Apparent, Minister of Personnel, and Grand Secretary of the Jinshen Hall.

translation_en:
Metropolitan Examination of the Eighth Year of Jiajing (1529)

Chief Administrators of the Examination

Fang Xianfu, Grand Master for Splendid Happiness, Pillar of State, Junior Guardian concurrently serving as Grand Guardian of the Heir Apparent, and Minister of Rites concurrently serving as Academician of the Hanlin Academy. His courtesy name was Shuxian; he was from Nanhai County, Guangdong, and was a metropolitan graduate (jinshi) of the yichou year.

Li Shi, Grand Master for Excellent Counsel and Left Vice Minister of Rites. His courtesy name was Zongyi; he was from Renqiu County, Zhili, and was a metropolitan graduate of the renxu year.

Examiners

Zhang Cong, Grand Master for Splendid Happiness, Pillar of State, Junior Preceptor concurrently serving as Grand Preceptor of the Heir Apparent, Minister of Personnel, and Grand Secretary of the Jinshen Hall. His courtesy name was Bingyong; he was from Yongjia County, Zhejiang, and was a metropolitan graduate of the xinsi year.

Huo Tao, Grand Master for Thorough Counsel and Supervisor of the Household of the Heir Apparent concurrently serving as Academician of the Hanlin Academy. His courtesy name was Weixian; he was from Nanhai County, Guangdong, and was a metropolitan graduate of the jiaxu year.

Associate Examiners

Liao Daonan, Gentleman for Straightforward Service and Right Rectifier in the Right Secretariat of the Heir Apparent. His courtesy name was Mingwu; he was from Puqi County, Huguang, and was a metropolitan graduate of the xinsi year.

Lun Yixun, Senior Compiler of the Hanlin Academy and Gentleman for Cultivated Learning. His courtesy name was Yanshi; he was from Nanhai County, Guangdong, and was a metropolitan graduate of the dingchou year.

Gong Yongqing, Senior Compiler of the Hanlin Academy and Gentleman for General Service. His courtesy name was Mingzhi; he was from Huai'an County, Fujian, and was a metropolitan graduate of the bingxu year.

Wang Yongbin, Senior Compiler of the Hanlin Academy and Gentleman for General Service. His courtesy name was Yunxing; he was from Xianning County, Shaanxi, and was a metropolitan graduate of the xinsi year.

Lin Wenjun, Gentleman for General Service and Right Admonisher in the Right Secretariat of the Heir Apparent. His courtesy name was Ruying; he was from Putian County, Fujian, and was a metropolitan graduate of the xinwei year.

Cai Ang, Gentleman for General Service and Right Admonisher in the Right Secretariat of the Heir Apparent. His courtesy name was Hengzhong; he was registered with the Huai'an Guard in Zhili, was a native of Jiading County, and was a metropolitan graduate of the jiaxu year.

Wang Jiao, Junior Compiler of the Hanlin Academy and Gentleman for Literary Service. His courtesy name was Yongzhi; he was from Xiangfu County, Henan, and was a metropolitan graduate of the guiwei year.

Zhang Xing, Junior Compiler of the Hanlin Academy and Gentleman for Literary Service. His courtesy name was Ziyang; he was registered with the Guilin Guard in Guangxi, was a native of Lingui County, and was a metropolitan graduate of the dingchou year.

Zhang Gun, Junior Compiler of the Hanlin Academy and Gentleman for Literary Service. His courtesy name was Buzhi; he was from Jiangyin County, Zhili, and was a metropolitan graduate of the xinsi year.

Yang Weijie, Junior Compiler of the Hanlin Academy and Gentleman for Rendering Service. His courtesy name was Yingfu; he was from Gu'an County, Shuntian Prefecture, and was a metropolitan graduate of the bingxu year.

translation_en:
Jin Lu, Compiler in the Hanlin Academy, had the courtesy name Meizhi and was from Qiantang County, Zhejiang. He became a metropolitan graduate (jinshi) in the bingxu year (1526).

Chen Gaomo, Chief Supervising Secretary in the Office of Scrutiny for Works, had the courtesy name Mingshi. He was registered with Zhenwu Guard, Shanxi, and was a native of Daizhou. He became a metropolitan graduate in the xinsi year (1521).

Li Heming, Gentleman for Distinguished Service and Supervising Secretary in the Office of Scrutiny for Personnel, had the courtesy name Jiugao and was from Yiwu County, Zhejiang. He became a metropolitan graduate in the dingchou year (1517).

Wang Zhun, Supervising Secretary in the Office of Scrutiny for Rites, had the courtesy name Zitui. He was registered with the Ceremonial Guard Office in Shaanxi and was a native of Shanyin County, Zhejiang. He became a metropolitan graduate in the guiwei year (1523).

Chen Ru, Gentleman for Rendering Virtuous Service and Secretary acting as Director of the Guangxi Bureau in the Ministry of Revenue, had the courtesy name Maoxue. He belonged to an officer household registered with the Embroidered-uniform Guard and became a metropolitan graduate in the guiwei year (1523).

Li Mo, Gentleman for Rendering Virtuous Service and Secretary acting as Vice Director of the Bureau of Merit in the Ministry of Personnel, had the courtesy name Shiyan and was from Ouning County, Fujian. He became a metropolitan graduate in the xinsi year (1521).

Huang Zhen, Gentleman for Rendering Virtuous Service and Secretary in the Bureau of Military Operations in the Ministry of War, had the courtesy name Dezhao and was from Anqiu County, Shandong. He became a metropolitan graduate in the guiwei year (1523).

Examination Inspectors:

Liu Lian, Gentleman of the Literary Forest and Investigating Censor for the Yunnan Circuit, had the courtesy name Junbo and was from Nangong County, Zhili. He became a metropolitan graduate in the xinsi year (1521).

Zhou Xu, Investigating Censor for the Huguang Circuit, had the courtesy name Qihe and was from Anfu County, Jiangxi. He became a metropolitan graduate in the xinsi year (1521).

Proctors:

Lu Tang, Gentleman for Rendering Virtuous Service and Secretary acting as Vice Director of the Bureau of Ceremonies in the Ministry of Rites, had the courtesy name Kentang and was from Changshu County, Zhili. He became a metropolitan graduate in the guiwei year (1523).

Sun Ang, Gentleman for Straightforward Service and Secretary in the Bureau of Receptions in the Ministry of Rites, had the courtesy name Yihe and was from Changyi County, Shandong. He became a metropolitan graduate in the xinsi year (1521).

Officials Responsible for Printing Examination Papers:

Fang Lan, Gentleman for Rendering Virtuous Service and Secretary acting as Director of the Bureau of Ceremonies in the Ministry of Rites, had the courtesy name Shipei and was from Putian County, Fujian. He became a metropolitan graduate in the guiwei year (1523).

Ouyang Shu, Gentleman for Straightforward Service and Secretary in the Bureau of Ceremonies in the Ministry of Rites, had the courtesy name Chongru and was from Taihe County, Jiangxi. He became a metropolitan graduate in the bingxu year (1526).

Officials Responsible for Collecting and Keeping Examination Scripts:

Li Qi, Gentleman for Distinguished Service and Central Drafting Office Secretary, had the courtesy name Yuzhong. He belonged to an officer household registered with Longmen Battalion in Xuanfu and was a native of Hezhou, Zhili. He became a tribute student (gongshi) in the jimao year (1519).

Wu Yin, Grand Master of Central Accord and Vice Prefect of Xiangyang Prefecture, Huguang, had the courtesy name Jingfu. He was from Changshu County in the directly administered metropolitan region (Zhili), and was a tribute scholar (gongshi) of the yimao year.

Four Books

Yan Yuan said, “May I ask for the particulars?” The Master said, “Do not look at what is contrary to ritual propriety; do not listen to what is contrary to ritual propriety; do not say what is contrary to ritual propriety; do not do what is contrary to ritual propriety.” Yan Yuan said, “Though I, Hui, am not quick to understand, allow me to put these words into practice.”

Only one possessed of the utmost sincerity under Heaven can order the great guiding relationships of the world, establish its great foundation, and understand the transforming and nurturing processes of Heaven and Earth. On what could such a person depend?

Confucius was the sage whose actions accorded with the time.

Book of Changes

This is the way of Earth, the way of a wife, and the way of a minister. The way of Earth is not to claim achievement of its own, but to bring things to completion on behalf of another.

“Someone augments it”: this comes from outside.

Heaven has five numbers, and Earth has five numbers. The five positions correspond to one another, and each has its complement. Heaven’s numbers total twenty-five, and Earth’s numbers total thirty. Together, the numbers of Heaven and Earth total fifty-five. Through these, changes and transformations are accomplished and the spirits are set in operation. The number of the Great Expansion is fifty, of which forty-nine are used. Divide them into two heaps to represent the two powers, Heaven and Earth; set one stalk apart between the fingers to represent the three powers, Heaven, Earth, and humanity; count them off by fours to represent the four seasons; and place the remainder between the fingers to represent an intercalary month. translation_en:
…then suspend a stalk. The stalks of Qian number two hundred and sixteen; those of Kun, one hundred and forty-four. Together they number three hundred and sixty, corresponding to the days of a year. The stalks of the two parts of the Changes number eleven thousand five hundred and twenty, corresponding to the number of the myriad things.
The Yellow Emperor, Yao, and Shun let their upper and lower garments hang down, and all under Heaven was well governed. They presumably took this from Qian and Kun.

Book of Documents
Be cautious and diligent: in a single day or two, there are ten thousand incipient affairs to attend to.
He who cultivates himself and whose genuine virtue brings harmony to those below is an enlightened ruler. The former king cared for the distressed and impoverished as his children. The people obeyed his commands, and none were displeased. Even the neighboring rulers of states said: “We await our sovereign; when our sovereign comes, there will be no punishment.” O king, exert yourself in virtue and look to your illustrious ancestor; never indulge in ease or indolence. In serving your ancestors, think of filial devotion; in dealing with those below, think of respect. Discernment consists in seeing far; keen hearing consists in listening to virtue. I shall uphold your excellence, O king, without wearying.
When the moon follows the stars, wind and rain result.
Reverently make your instructions clear, thereby following the former kings, acknowledging and extolling the glorious mandate of Kings Wen and Wu, and matching the achievements of your predecessors.

…the marsh. Those men are building walls; a hundred stretches of wall rise together. Though they toil, in the end they will dwell in peace.

Tai Si continued the tradition of excellent repute; thus she had a hundred sons.

Hard-pressed are the heads of the various offices; careworn is the Grand Steward! The directors of horses, preceptors, provisioners, and attendants on either side—none fails to attend fully to his duties; none is unequal to his task.

It is late spring: what more do we seek? How fare the newly reclaimed fields and those in their third year of cultivation? Ah, splendid wheat and barley! We shall receive that bright blessing. The radiant Lord on High will at last grant a year of abundance.

行一物而三善皆得者，唯世子而已，其齒於學之謂也。故世子齒於學，國人觀之，曰：「將君我而與我齒讓，何也？」曰：「有父在，則禮然。」然而衆知父子之道矣。其二曰：「將君我而與我齒讓，何也？」曰：「有君在，則禮然。」然而衆著於君臣之義也。其三曰：「將君我而與我齒讓，何也？」曰：「長長也。」然而衆知長幼之節矣。

言語之美，穆穆皇皇；朝廷之美，濟濟翔翔；祭祀之美，齊齊皇皇；車馬之美，匪匪翼翼；鸞和之美，肅肅雍雍。

此四者，心之莫同也。知其心，然後能救其失也。教也者，長善而救其失者也。

第貳場

論

聖人立人極
translation_en:
When standing, one bends like a chime stone, letting one’s pendants hang down. When the lord’s pendants hang at an angle, the minister’s hang straight down; when the lord’s hang straight down, the minister’s reach the ground.

Only the heir apparent can perform a single act and thereby attain all three virtues: this refers to his taking his place according to age at school. Thus, when the heir apparent takes his place according to age at school, the people of the state observe him and say, “He is to be our ruler, yet he yields to us according to age. Why?” The answer is, “While his father lives, ritual propriety requires it.” Thus the multitude comes to understand the Way governing father and son. Secondly, they say, “He is to be our ruler, yet he yields to us according to age. Why?” The answer is, “While his ruler lives, ritual propriety requires it.” Thus the multitude comes to recognize clearly the proper relationship between ruler and minister. Thirdly, they say, “He is to be our ruler, yet he yields to us according to age. Why?” The answer is, “He is honoring his elders.” Thus the multitude comes to understand the distinctions between elder and younger.

The beauty of speech lies in its reverence and dignity; the beauty of the court, in its orderly bearing and graceful movement; the beauty of sacrifices, in their reverence and splendor; the beauty of chariots and horses, in their ordered movement and coordination; and the beauty of the luan and he carriage bells, in their solemn and harmonious sound.

These four types differ in their dispositions. Only after understanding their dispositions can one remedy their faults. Teaching means fostering what is good and remedying their faults.

Second Session

Discourse

The sage establishes the supreme standard for humanity.

translation_en:
…these chapters are surviving remnants of the auspicious ceremonies; the chapters on diplomatic visits and audiences with the sovereign are surviving remnants of the guest ceremonies; and the chapters on funerals for officers, post-burial sacrifices for officers, and the rites following the evening observance are surviving remnants of the mourning ceremonies. Why alone are military ceremonies not recorded? Among the scholars of the Song and Yuan dynasties, some treated the Ceremonies and Rites (Yili) as the canonical text and the Record of Rites (Liji) as its commentary. Others assembled a Comprehensive Explanation (Tongjie) or compiled a Lost Canon of the Ceremonies and Rites (Yili yijing). Were these sufficient to fill the gaps in the ritual institutions recorded in the Offices of Zhou (Zhouguan)? Or did they offer further insights through which these works mutually elucidate one another? At the beginning of the Hongwu reign of our dynasty, Confucian court scholars were commanded to compile the Collected Rites of the Great Ming (Da Ming jili). It contains fourteen categories of sacrificial ceremonies, five of auspicious ceremonies, two of guest ceremonies, three of military ceremonies, and two of mourning ceremonies. Do these accord with the ancient rites or not? May we hear what the Confucian court scholars of that time investigated and what the ritual officials determined in detail? Our Emperor governs all under Heaven through filial piety and seeks to establish the realm in benevolence, righteousness, rites, and music. Education through rites is, moreover, a task that must take priority today. You candidates should explain its essentials in detail, as an offering to the sovereign.

問：道德一而後風俗同。士習不正，則道德不一，欲風俗之同難矣。故自古論治必
translation_en:
…and brought about good government through strenuous effort: these rulers cannot all be judged alike. Emperor Wen of Han and Emperor Renzong of Song were both rulers who governed through reverent self-composure. Did they fully realize the way of preserving an inherited achievement? Did the ministers who submitted proposals at the time contribute to the good government of these two rulers? How did rulers who exerted themselves strenuously, such as Emperor Xuan of Han and Emperor Shenzong of Song, compare with Emperor Wen and Emperor Renzong? One laid the foundations of calamity; the other brewed the disorders of the Jingkang era. The appointments and actions of these two rulers are all recorded in the histories: where, precisely, did their successes and failures lie? Why do the ruler who preserved the institutions of the Han house and the ruler who transformed the government incur the same criticism?

Now our sage and enlightened sovereign reigns above, vigorously rousing himself and seeking to accomplish his great undertaking. Weighing past and present and considering what is appropriate to the times, what course should he follow? The plans by which our sagely progenitor bequeathed peace to his descendants for countless ages surely require no meddlesome alteration. Yet can there be nothing that has fallen into disuse and ought to be restored? Everyone knows that meddlesome alteration and restoration are different. Unless one examines affairs from their origins through their ramifications, however, there are matters difficult to pronounce upon where the two appear deceptively similar. To put strenuous effort into practice and thereby achieve government through reverent self-composure, what should be put in order? We wish to hear a discussion that reaches the foundations and the essentials of principle.

Question: Only after moral principles are unified can customs become uniform. If the habits of scholars are not upright, moral principles will not be unified, and it will be difficult to make customs uniform. Thus, from antiquity, discussions of government have necessarily…

…give priority to nurturing scholars, for as scholars’ conduct declines or improves, the fortunes of the state follow: the stakes are of the utmost importance. Our dynasty has established schools and methods of selection and performance assessment to nurture scholars. These have been studied and refined year after year and month after month, becoming more thorough than those of antiquity. Why, then, has the tendency toward frivolity and competitive pursuit of advancement still not ceased? One might attribute it to the times. Yet with a sage and enlightened sovereign on the throne, even ordinary people are stirred to better themselves. I cannot believe that scholars should fall short of ordinary people. Among those of the past who discussed the ethos of scholars well, none surpassed Master Cheng of Yichuan and Master Chen of Houshan. Their views can be consulted in Policy Questions for an Examination at the Hanzhou School and Letter to Lin, Prefect of Xiuzhou. Do their arguments apply to the present? We now desire that what scholars cultivate should be pure, free of frivolous habits, and that what they uphold should be upright, free of competitive pursuit of advancement. We have considered how to achieve this but have not found the means. Please explain clearly.

===
問戍天下之治有幾通天下之變有權夫
幾者時之會也權者義之宜也二者勢
未嘗不相値而用常相須古昔帝王之
治天下其相時審幾據經行權以成一
代之化者載諸往籍古人亦論之詳矣
punctuated:
怠無荒，四夷來王；明王慎德，四夷咸賓。帝王之馭夷狄，固自有道。或謂高宗伐荆楚，周宣伐淮夷，皆稱中興，豈中葉德衰乃用武歟？抑守成之君，武事不可廢歟？我太祖高皇帝汛掃胡元，肅清華夏。太宗繼之，振揚光烈。東夷、西戎、南蠻、北狄，經畧之勤，餘二十年，曲防周慮，可謂至矣。厥後黎季犛之變，棄交阯；土魯番之侵，失哈密。不知我祖宗所以貽謀者何如？試舉商周漢唐之跡，斟酌之，為今日籌邊之助。

問：成天下之治有幾，通天下之變有權。夫幾者，時之會也；權者，義之宜也。二者勢未嘗不相值，而用常相須。古昔帝王之治天下，其相時審幾、據經行權，以成一代之化者，載諸往籍，古人亦論之詳矣。
translation_en:
… [Be without] negligence or idleness, and the peoples of the four quarters will come to acknowledge your kingship; when an enlightened king attends carefully to his virtue, the peoples of the four quarters all come as guests. Emperors and kings assuredly have their own proper way of governing the foreign peoples. Some say that Gaozong’s campaign against Jing-Chu and King Xuan of Zhou’s campaign against the Huai peoples were both acclaimed as dynastic restorations. Was it because virtue declined midway through these dynasties that they resorted to force? Or is military preparedness something that rulers preserving an inherited realm cannot abandon? Our Emperor Taizu Gao swept away the non-Chinese Yuan and thoroughly pacified the Chinese realm. Taizong succeeded him and magnified his glorious achievements. For more than twenty years he labored to manage the eastern Yi, western Rong, southern Man, and northern Di. His precautions against every contingency and his comprehensive deliberations may be called consummate. Subsequently, after the upheaval of Li Jili, Jiaozhi was abandoned; following the invasion by Tulufan, Hami was lost. What, then, were the plans our imperial ancestors bequeathed to their successors? Discuss and weigh the precedents of Shang, Zhou, Han, and Tang, to assist present-day planning for the frontiers.

Question: Bringing order to the realm depends on discerning incipient opportunities; responding effectively to changes throughout the realm depends on discretionary judgment. Incipient opportunity is the convergence of circumstances at a particular time; discretionary judgment is what righteousness makes appropriate. These two always coincide in the circumstances that arise, and their application always requires each other. The ways in which emperors and kings of antiquity governed the realm—assessing the times and discerning incipient opportunities, grounding themselves in constant principles while exercising discretion, and thereby bringing about the moral transformation of an age—are recorded in earlier writings. The ancients also discussed them in detail.

title: 嘉靖八年會試錄
text:
不知當時何所審尚而後可以正始不
至於病終何所損益而後可以範今不
至於泥古夫執樞以運持衡以平非君
德之明且剛弗能也我
皇上神明之智乾健之德正足以當斯二者不
知
今日之幾何以轉移而成化
今日之權何以通變而不窮其要目安在請
明言以驗匡濟之畧

punctuated: 不知當時何所審尚，而後可以正始，不至於病終？何所損益，而後可以範今，不至於泥古？夫執樞以運，持衡以平，非君德之明且剛弗能也。我皇上神明之智、乾健之德，正足以當斯二者。不知今日之幾，何以轉移而成化？今日之權，何以通變而不窮？其要目安在？請明言，以驗匡濟之畧。
translation_en: …What did they carefully assess and esteem in their time, so as to set matters right at the outset and avoid troubles at the end? What did they diminish or augment, so as to provide a model for the present without becoming bound to antiquity? To grasp the pivot and set things in motion, to hold the balance and bring things into equilibrium—these require a ruler whose virtue is both discerning and firm. Our Emperor’s divinely perspicacious wisdom and Heaven-like vigor are fully sufficient for these two tasks. How, then, can the critical opportunities of the present be turned to account to bring about transformation? How can discretionary judgment today respond to changing circumstances without reaching an impasse? Where do the essential points lie? Explain these clearly, so that your strategies for setting affairs right and bringing aid to the realm may be assessed.

Tang Shunzhi

title: 嘉靖八年會試錄
text:
我者也而人之自遠乎仁者以其有非禮存焉
爾夫人莫不有視聽也物交於外則引之而已
矣爾於非禮者勿視焉勿聽焉所以防其自外
入而動於內也夫人莫不有言動也欲動于內
則肆焉而已矣爾於非禮者勿言焉勿動焉所
以謹其自內出而接乎外也夫如是則心德全
而仁在是矣顏子遂言曰回也䘏不聰非曰能
之夫子道至大實願學焉夫仁與不仁之幾在

translation_en:
…what Heaven has bestowed upon us. People distance themselves from humaneness only because something contrary to ritual propriety remains within them. Everyone sees and hears; when external things come into contact with them, they are simply drawn along. Look at nothing contrary to ritual propriety, and listen to nothing contrary to ritual propriety: this guards against what enters from outside and stirs within. Everyone speaks and acts; when desires stir within, they simply give them free rein. Say nothing contrary to ritual propriety, and do nothing contrary to ritual propriety: this exercises care over what issues from within and engages with the outside. If you do this, the virtue of the heart will be whole, and humaneness will reside therein.”

Master Yan then said: “I, Hui, though [?] not quick of understanding, do not claim to be capable of this. Your Way, Master, is supremely great, and I truly wish to learn it.” The critical distinction between humaneness and its absence lies simply between refraining and failing to refrain. To turn back at this point is to accord with Heaven’s principle; to drift onward from it is to follow human desires. Thus these words, [illegible passage], fully encompass the work of practicing humaneness; extended far enough to be tested throughout the world, they also bring to its utmost the effect of all turning toward humaneness. Truly, one should cherish them earnestly in one’s heart and devote oneself to their practice.

Here we can see that Master Yan’s consummate clarity sufficed to discern the incipient turning point, and his consummate strength sufficed to carry his resolve into effect. Although the Way of humaneness is supremely great, he was ultimately able not to depart from it for three months. Was this not because he was sincere in this practice and had attained something through it? Nevertheless, among the disciples of Confucius who asked about humaneness, none received an explanation so detailed as this. On another occasion, when he asked about governing a state, Confucius also weighed the rites and music of the four dynasties in instructing him. Humaneness is the virtue of Heaven; rites and music are the Way of kings. Hence the saying: “With the virtue of Heaven, one may then speak of the Way of kings.”

聖人之能事，一無所事者也。夫勉而為者，非聖人之能也。宜《中庸》舉此以發明天道也歟！蓋謂無妄之謂誠，動以天為無妄，動以人則妄矣。故唯天下至誠，乃能以渾然之實德，發而為自然之功用。孰不為道，而民彝乃率性之道，是之謂大經。聖人經綸之，而五典惇焉，五禮庸焉，天下之人庸外此而他法乎？孰不為性，而降衷乃天命之性，是之謂大本。聖人立之，而萬善足焉，萬化出焉，天下之道庸舍此而他由乎？至於天地
translation_en:
“Only one possessed of the utmost sincerity under Heaven can order the great enduring relationships of the world, establish the great foundation of the world, and understand the transforming and nourishing operations of Heaven and Earth. On what, then, would he depend?”

Wang Chong

Associate Examiner Li, Supervising Secretary, comments: “Refined and elegant; worthy of emulation.” Associate Examiner Zhang, Hanlin Compiler, comments: “The meaning is clearly conveyed and the diction dignified.” Associate Examiner Cai, Right Admonisher, comments: “Precise and pertinent.” Associate Examiner Lin, Right Admonisher, comments: “Concise in wording and complete in meaning.” Examiner Huo, Academician, comments: “Grasps the purport.” Examiner Zhang, Grand Secretary, comments: “Pertinent and substantial.”

The sage’s accomplishments require no deliberate exertion whatsoever. What is done through strenuous effort is not the sage’s distinctive capacity. How fitting that the Doctrine of the Mean should bring this forward to illuminate the Way of Heaven! For sincerity means freedom from falsity: to act through Heaven is to be free from falsity; to act through human contrivance is to fall into falsity. Thus only one possessed of the utmost sincerity under Heaven can manifest his integral, genuine virtue in its spontaneous workings.

What is not an expression of the Way? Yet the enduring norms of human relations are the Way of following one’s nature: these are called the great enduring relationships. The sage orders them, so that the five cardinal relationships are strengthened and the five rites put into practice. Could the people of the world go beyond these and take something else as their model?

What is not an expression of nature? Yet the inner moral constitution bestowed from above is the nature conferred by Heaven: this is called the great foundation. The sage establishes it, so that all goodness is complete within it and all transformations issue from it. Could the ways of the world abandon this and proceed by some other course? 化育，是命也，又大經大本之所自出也。聖人知天地之化育，則純一不已，與於穆不已脗合無間矣。夫惟經綸天下之大經，是能致和也；立天下之大本，是能致中也；知天地之化育，又能窮理以至於命也。盖其出也以誠，不以妄；其動也以天，不以人。體信以達順，固有不依形而立者焉；誠精而神應，固有不恃勢而行者焉。夫何倚著之有？噫！至誠無妄，自然之功用於此可見矣。抑考《中庸》，首曰命，曰性，曰道，此則曰道，曰性，而後曰命者，何也？先儒胡氏謂：「首章由造化說聖人，由體之隱達於用之費也；此章言聖人之所以為造化，由用之費而原其體之隱也。」斯言得之矣。

translation_en:
…the transformation and nourishment [of Heaven and Earth]: this is the Mandate, and it is also the source from which the great guiding principles and the great foundation emerge. When the sage knows the transforming and nourishing activity of Heaven and Earth, his unceasing purity and unity accord without any interval with their profound, unceasing operation. Ordering the great guiding principles of the world means being able to bring harmony to its fullest realization; establishing the great foundation of the world means being able to bring equilibrium to its fullest realization; knowing the transforming and nourishing activity of Heaven and Earth further means being able to investigate principle exhaustively and thereby arrive at the Mandate. For what issues forth from him proceeds through sincerity, not falsity; his actions proceed through Heaven, not human contrivance. Embodying trustworthiness and thereby attaining accord, he possesses that which stands without depending on physical form. His sincerity is refined and evokes a spiritual response, so he possesses that which operates without relying on power. What dependence could there be? Ah! Here one can see the spontaneous efficacy of utmost sincerity, free from falsity.

Yet consider the Doctrine of the Mean: at its beginning it speaks of the Mandate, then human nature, then the Way; here it speaks of the Way, then human nature, and only afterward the Mandate. Why is this? The earlier Confucian scholar Hu said: “The opening chapter proceeds from the workings of creation to explain the sage, moving from the hiddenness of substance to the breadth of its functioning. This chapter speaks of how the sage participates in the workings of creation, tracing the breadth of functioning back to its hidden substance.” These words have grasped the meaning.

“Confucius was the sage who acted according to the time.”
By Su Yinglin 粟應麟.

The sage is one who establishes the great Mean. The Way takes the Mean as its highest attainment; to attain the Mean is to act in accordance with the time. Who but Confucius could attain this? Mencius described the three sages and concluded with Confucius, thereby establishing the standard for the learning of the sages. Thus Bo Yi, Yi Yin, and Liu Xiahui were all sages of antiquity, but each embodied only one aspect of sagehood. Confucius was the sage of timeliness. Accordingly, whether he took office or withdrew, remained long or departed swiftly, he had neither preconceived notions nor rigid insistence; he held neither that something must be done nor that it must not be done. He changed with the times to follow the Way, moving with the times in response to Heaven. He combined the conduct of Bo Yi, Yi Yin, and Liu Xiahui, bringing each into play at the appropriate time. Consider the Five Phases: the three sages each embodied the operation of one; was Confucius not the Supreme Ultimate in its entirety, wondrously setting the Five Phases in motion without leaving a trace? He united the ways of purity, responsibility, and harmony, putting each into practice at the appropriate time. Consider the four seasons: the three sages each embodied the vital energy of one; was Confucius not the primal vital energy of Supreme Harmony, circulating through the four seasons without exhaustion? Thus it is said: “Confucius was the sage of timeliness.” He possessed every goodness and attained Heaven’s virtue: this is what made his Way great. Yet did Confucius merely unite in himself Bo Yi, Yi Yin, and Liu Xiahui? In dreaming of the Duke of Zhou, he also embraced the Duke of Zhou. In transmitting the traditions of Yao and Shun and taking Wen and Wu as his models, he also embraced Yao, Shun, Wen, and Wu. In taking Heaven above as his rule and following Earth below, he also embraced Heaven and Earth. This is what made his Way great. Yet Confucius was so intent on his endeavors that he forgot to eat; he loved antiquity and diligently sought it out; with restless urgency…

Kun does not dare to rival Qian, because their respective roles are fixed. That the Commentary sets out these distinctions one by one in this way exemplifies caution over the slightest beginnings. In Qian and Kun in the Book of Changes, yin and yang establish their positions; vigor and compliance constitute their natures; and firmness and yielding constitute their virtues. Kun is pure yin. text:
若疑於陽也在坤則三亦陰也陰有地道焉夫
妻之道健順盡之矣三之性若疑於健也在坤
則三亦順也順有妻道焉君臣之道剛柔盡之
矣三之德若疑於剛也在坤則三亦柔也柔有
臣道焉觀諸地道惟其分陰也故動闢之氣無
所事於直遂資生之德未嘗有于專成承乾之
氣代之以化光法之效者所以終夫象之成者
也因天之施代之以咸亨能之簡者所以終夫

===

punctuated:
若疑於陽也，在坤則三亦陰也，陰有地道焉。夫妻之道，健順盡之矣。三之性若疑於健也，在坤則三亦順也，順有妻道焉。君臣之道，剛柔盡之矣。三之德若疑於剛也，在坤則三亦柔也，柔有臣道焉。觀諸地道，惟其分陰也，故動闢之氣無所事於直遂，資生之德未嘗有于專成。承乾之氣，代之以化，光法之效者，所以終夫象之成者也；因天之施，代之以咸亨，能之簡者，所以終夫知之易者也。是地道則然也，况於妻道乎？况於臣道乎？六三之占，雖有美，含之以從王事，弗敢成也，分定故也。易之蘊也，文言之義，慎微也夫！抑君臣也，夫婦也，天地囿焉者也。臣干君，婦乘夫，天地亦遂以不位，天地因人者也。故曰：「人者，天地之心也。」坤，聖人至戒也。履霜，其始也；黃裳，其盛也；龍戰，其極也。慎之至也，扶焉抑焉，宰造化之力也。

黃帝堯舜垂衣裳而天下治，盖取諸乾坤。
莊用賓
translation_en:
…seems perhaps to belong to yang; within Kun, however, the third line is also yin, and yin embodies the way of Earth. The way of husband and wife is fully comprised in strength and compliance. The nature of the third line seems perhaps to be strength; within Kun, however, the third line is also compliant, and compliance embodies the way of the wife. The way of ruler and minister is fully comprised in firmness and yielding. The virtue of the third line seems perhaps to be firmness; within Kun, however, the third line is also yielding, and yielding embodies the way of the minister.

Consider the way of Earth. Precisely because its allotted role is yin, its vital force of movement and opening does not undertake to advance directly on its own, and its virtue of sustaining life never claims sole responsibility for bringing things to completion. Receiving Qian’s vital force, it effects transformation on Qian’s behalf: the efficacy of its radiant pattern [?] brings to completion the formation of images. Following Heaven’s bestowal, it brings universal flourishing on Heaven’s behalf: the simplicity of its capacity completes the ease of Heaven’s knowing. If this is so of the way of Earth, how much more so of the way of the wife! How much more so of the way of the minister! In the prognostication for six in the third place, though one possesses excellence, one keeps it concealed while serving the king’s affairs, not daring to claim achievement, because one’s allotted role is fixed. This is the profound import of the Changes; the meaning of the Commentary on the Words is surely vigilance over the slightest beginnings!

Moreover, the relations of ruler and minister, husband and wife, are those within which Heaven and Earth are encompassed. If a minister encroaches upon his ruler, or a wife dominates her husband, Heaven and Earth consequently lose their proper positions: Heaven and Earth depend upon human beings. Thus it is said, “Human beings are the heart of Heaven and Earth.” In Kun, the sage gives his most solemn warning. “Treading on frost” marks the beginning; “a yellow lower garment,” the flourishing stage; and “dragons battling,” the ultimate extreme. Such is the utmost vigilance! Supporting one and restraining the other: this is the power to govern the workings of creation.

“The Yellow Emperor, Yao, and Shun let their upper and lower garments hang down, and the world was well governed. They presumably took this from Qian and Kun.”
Zhuang Yongbin

The Great Commentary sets forth the sages’ spiritually luminous transformation, invariably tracing it to the Changes. For the Changes becomes manifest only through the sages: by observing their transforming influence, we see the true character of Qian and Kun. Now Huangdi, Yao, and Shun succeeded Fuxi and Shennong as rulers. Where they could not govern by following precedent, they adapted to the times. Thus, once the benefits of adaptation and change had been brought forth, institutions suited to the people were fully established; the efficacy of spiritual transformation was inexhaustible, and the embellishments of human culture were made manifest. Encompassed by the emperors’ power, the people were already inspired to flourish together and enjoy its benefits to the fullest. As the sages’ Way brought aid to all under Heaven, those above and below likewise moved in a common current, realizing spiritual efficacy to the fullest.
People saw them wearing dark upper garments and reddish-yellow lower garments to distinguish royal ceremonial forms, but did not understand that the means by which they illumined the lands in all four directions were likewise nothing more than this. People saw their upper garments embroidered with axe patterns and their yellow lower garments displaying luminous virtue, but did not understand that the means by which they harmonized the myriad states were likewise nothing more than this. How did this come about? I have examined it in the two hexagrams Qian and Kun. Qian and Kun contain the inner workings of creation and transformation; creation and transformation are the manifestation of change and movement. translation_en:
…the workings of opening, movement, and stillness operate silently, without conscious intent. Thus the sage takes these as his model. Heaven and Earth accomplish their work through what is naturally so; the sage establishes his teaching through the numinous Way. The proper time cannot be defied, and transformation cannot be forced. What need has the sage for deliberate contrivance? The Book of Changes speaks comprehensively of change and transformation: Ge (Revolution) speaks of the old, and Ding (The Cauldron) of the new; Xian (Influence) speaks of responsiveness, and Heng (Duration) of endurance. Without responsiveness, nothing can endure. Xu (Waiting) speaks of waiting: when the time is not right, one waits. Tai (Peace) can become Pi (Obstruction); only after Wei Ji (Before Completion) does completion come. These speak of their respective times. Skillful adaptation brings order; unskillful adaptation brings obstruction. It is simply a matter of examining the times.

title: 嘉靖八年會試錄
text:
謨于舜而推本於君身如此蓋謂人君以一人
之身臨兆民之衆崇高矣而非可安之地也其
得不兢兢矣乎尊榮矣而非可樂之地也其得
不業業矣乎蓋成天下之務惟幾也而隳天下
之務亦幾也幾也者發動之所由也善惡之所
由分也一念不謹或以貽四海之憂一日不謹
或以致千百年之患而况一日二日焉有萬幾
焉紛然而至其何以應之沓然而來其何以處
之故非至明不能以察之非至健不能以决之

警之也至矣觀帝庸作歌曰敕天之命惟時惟

事幾暴著猶不知省及至禍機激發始思所以
圖之亦末如之何矣噫可鑒也夫

不業業矣乎盖成天下之務惟幾也而隳天下
之務亦幾也幾也者發動之所由也善惡之所
由分也一念不謹或以貽四海之憂一日不謹
或以致千百年之患而况一日二日焉有萬幾
焉紛然而至其何以應之沓然而來其何以處
之欽非至明不能以察之非至健不能以決之
===
圖難於易猶恐甚難兢兢其可已乎為大於細
猶恐將大業業其可已乎噫臯陶以是告帝其
警之也至矣觀帝庸作歌曰勑天之命惟時惟
幾則幾之一言虞廷君臣交相戒飭誠保治之
樞要也先儒真氏謂後世人主不此之戒故雖
事幾暴著猶不知省及至禍機激發始思所以
圖之亦末如之何矣噫可鑒也夫
爾惟敬明乃訓用奉若于先王對揚文武
之光命追配于前人
punctuated:
謨于舜，而推本於君身如此。蓋謂人君以一人之身，臨兆民之衆，崇高矣，而非可安之地也，其得不兢兢矣乎？尊榮矣，而非可樂之地也，其得不業業矣乎？蓋成天下之務惟幾也，而隳天下之務亦幾也。幾也者，發動之所由也，善惡之所由分也。一念不謹，或以貽四海之憂；一日不謹，或以致千百年之患。而况一日二日焉有萬幾焉，紛然而至，其何以應之？沓然而來，其何以處之？故非至明不能以察之，非至健不能以决之。圖難於易，猶恐甚難，兢兢其可已乎？為大於細，猶恐將大，業業其可已乎？噫！臯陶以是告帝，其警之也至矣。觀帝庸作歌曰：「敕天之命，惟時惟幾。」則幾之一言，虞廷君臣交相戒飭，誠保治之樞要也。先儒真氏謂後世人主不此之戒，故雖事幾暴著，猶不知省；及至禍機激發，始思所以圖之，亦末如之何矣。噫！可鑒也夫！

爾惟敬明乃訓，用奉若于先王，對揚文武之光命，追配于前人。
translation_en:
…counsel to Shun, thus tracing its foundation back to the ruler himself. The meaning is that the ruler, in his single person, presides over the multitude of his subjects. His position is lofty, yet it is no place for ease: how could he fail to be vigilant? His position is honored and glorious, yet it is no place for pleasure: how could he fail to be apprehensive? For the accomplishment of the world's affairs depends on incipient impulses, and their ruin likewise depends on them. These impulses are where action originates and where good and evil diverge. A single heedless thought may bequeath sorrow to all within the Four Seas; a single heedless day may bring calamities lasting hundreds or thousands of years. Moreover, within one or two days there are ten thousand such beginnings. As they arrive in confusion, how can he respond? As they come one upon another, how can he handle them? Thus, only utmost discernment can perceive them, and only utmost vigor can resolve them. Even when planning for difficulties while matters are still easy, he fears that they may become exceedingly difficult: can his vigilance cease? Even when undertaking great matters while they are still small, he fears that they will grow great: can his apprehension cease?

Ah! Gao Yao's admonition to the emperor was most searching. Consider how the emperor thereupon composed a song, saying: “Attend reverently to Heaven's mandate; attend to the proper time and to incipient impulses.” Thus, in the single word “incipience,” ruler and ministers at the court of Yu mutually admonished one another. It is indeed the crucial means of preserving good government. The earlier Confucian scholar Master Zhen said that rulers of later ages failed to heed this warning. Consequently, even when the incipient tendencies of events were starkly apparent, they still did not know to reflect. Only when the forces of calamity erupted did they begin to think how to deal with them, but by then there was nothing they could do. Ah! This offers a lesson indeed!

Reverently make your instructions clear, thereby complying with the former kings, acknowledging and extolling the glorious mandate of Kings Wen and Wu, and emulating your predecessors.

賢王勉大臣修職，惟求世德而已。蓋前人之德，後人所當嗣焉者也。茍非恪修其職，豈世臣之謂乎？穆王命君牙，蓋謂文武之謨烈，一代之光命也。我先王成康嘗對揚之，而爾之祖父亦預有助矣。顧在今日，可使其無傳耶？然爾不必遠有所慕也，惟於我之訓爾者而敬明之，凡所以敷典和則以化夫民者，無有乎弗盡焉；以爾之所受於我者而懋昭之，凡所以思艱圖易以寧夫民者，無有乎弗恪焉。以若所為而仰質乎先猷，于成康有以奉順而不背，由此而上以對揚乎文武，其謨烈益以振厲而有光。如是，則爾之

When a worthy king exhorts his great ministers to fulfill their offices, he seeks only the perpetuation of ancestral virtue. For the virtue of predecessors is what their descendants ought to carry on. Unless a man conscientiously fulfills his office, how can he be called a hereditary minister?

When King Mu charged Jun Ya, his meaning was this: the plans and achievements of Kings Wen and Wu constituted the glorious mandate of their dynasty. Our former kings, Cheng and Kang, once acknowledged and extolled it, and your forebears also took part in supporting them. Yet today, can we allow it to go without a successor? You need not, however, seek distant objects of admiration. You need only reverently elucidate the instructions I give you, leaving nothing undone in promulgating the canonical teachings and harmonizing the standards, so as to transform the people. Strive to make manifest what you have received from me, neglecting nothing in considering difficulties and planning for ease, so as to bring peace to the people.

If you measure your conduct against the plans of our predecessors, you will thereby honor and follow Cheng and Kang without departing from their ways. translation_en:
…your duties will have been fulfilled. What cause, then, would you have to feel ashamed before your predecessors? The example your forebears set in loyalty to their ruler remains fully evident, and the legacy of their devoted service to the state still endures. If you can match your predecessors, then, although I am not a ruler like the former kings, I shall nevertheless have a minister like theirs. Why, then, could the government of the former kings not be restored?” Ah! How profound were King Mu’s expectations of Jun Ya!

Now, in expressing his hopes for King Cheng, the Duke of Zhou said: “Look upon King Wen’s brilliant light, and exalt King Wu’s great achievements.” In charging Jun Ya, King Mu said: “Do not disgrace your forebears; follow the path your forebears trod.” From this we know that ministers, in their expectations of their ruler, regard emulating his ancestors as the mark of sagehood; rulers, in what they demand of their ministers, particularly regard virtue transmitted through the generations as the mark of worthiness. This is why Zhou’s government flourished. When the poems Ban and Dang appeared and the ruler’s virtue declined, Grand Master Yin wielded power, and relatives by marriage occupied high office. Even hereditary ministers could no longer be relied upon. If we consult the Book of Odes to observe the changes of the age, should we not silently take to heart the instructions and proclamations of the Book of Documents?

有其德而獲其應，賢妃然也。夫內治有關於君德也尚矣。賢妃有婦順之德，而獲多男之應如此，謂不有助於文王之德者乎？詩人推本之意，蓋謂我文王德之盛也，成之固由乎大任之聖，助之亦由乎大姒之賢。何則？以大姒視大任，猶之大任視大姜也。蓋其恭敬之德，無間于思齊之姑；和樂之休，有光于思媚之婦。以似以續，德音孔嘉也。此人此德，世不常有也。由是衆妾樂其德，百男發其祥。德之所在，為賢為聖；位之所在，宜君宜王。郇霍魯衛，皆祚胤也，而宗支繁；郜雍曹滕，皆藩屏也，而根本固。於此見麟趾之化，為關雎之應，則大姒之賢，信有助於文王之德者深矣。抑觀之《易》曰：「坤厚載物，德合无疆。」又曰：「地道无成，而代有終也。」為此詩者，其知道乎！故繼之曰：「刑于寡妻，至于兄弟，以御于家邦。」蓋閨

To possess virtue and obtain its corresponding reward: so it was with this worthy consort. The connection between the ordering of the inner household and the ruler’s virtue is of ancient standing. This worthy consort possessed the virtue of wifely compliance and received in response so many sons. Could one say that she did not aid King Wen’s virtue? In tracing matters to their source, the poet meant that the fullness of our King Wen’s virtue was certainly formed through the sageliness of Tai Ren 大任 and was also aided by the worthiness of Tai Si 大姒. Why so? Tai Si’s relationship to Tai Ren was just like Tai Ren’s relationship to Tai Jiang 大姜. Her virtue of reverence and respect equaled that of the mother-in-law praised as “dignified”; the excellence of her harmony and joy brought added luster to the wife praised as “beloved.” Emulating and continuing their example, she enjoyed a most admirable reputation for virtue. Such a person and such virtue are not often found in the world. Thus the concubines delighted in her virtue, and a hundred sons manifested her auspicious reward. In virtue, they were worthy men and sages; in station, they were fit to be lords and kings. Xun, Huo, Lu, and Wei were all blessed descendants, and the branches of the lineage flourished; Gao, Yong, Cao, and Teng were all protective bulwarks, and the foundations stood firm. Here we see that the transforming influence celebrated in “The Qilin’s Hooves” was the response to “The Ospreys.” Tai Si’s worthiness thus assuredly gave profound assistance to King Wen’s virtue.

Consider also what the Book of Changes says: “Kun, in its thickness, bears all things; its virtue accords with the boundless.” It also says: “The way of earth claims no achievement, yet brings things to completion on another’s behalf.” Surely the composer of this poem understood the Way! Hence he continued: “He set an example for his wife, extended it to his brothers, and thereby governed his household and state.” For within the inner quarters…

title: 嘉靖八年會試錄
text:
時復何求歟彼新田始成而用力難今何如哉
無謂其難也者而鹵莽為也畬田已熟而用力
易今何如哉無謂其易也者而滅裂為也夫貽
我來牟乃帝命率育也今焉麥秋將至農乃登
麥則可以受上帝之明賜矣歲其有占乎自天
降康則豐年穰穰也由是年穀用成農乃登穀
又將賜我新畬以豐年矣歲其有望乎夫時易
失也不可以不勤效易見也不可以不勉周王
重農有如此者可謂知先務之為急矣說者謂
===
此為成王之詩也盖周家以農事開國故周公
告成王其見于詩有若七月其見于書有若無
逸欲其知稼穡之艱難與小人之依也厥後宣
王不藉千畝而虢公諫之於乎觀虢公之所以
諫則知周公之所以憂矣
春秋
夏六月公會齊侯宋公陳侯鄭伯同盟于
幽莊公二十有七年

時，復何求歟？彼新田始成而用力難，今何如哉？無謂其難也者而鹵莽為也。畬田已熟而用力易，今何如哉？無謂其易也者而滅裂為也。夫貽我來牟，乃帝命率育也。今焉麥秋將至，農乃登麥，則可以受上帝之明賜矣。歲其有占乎？自天降康，則豐年穰穰也。由是年穀用成，農乃登穀，又將賜我新畬以豐年矣。歲其有望乎？夫時易失也，不可以不勤；效易見也，不可以不勉。周王重農有如此者，可謂知先務之為急矣。說者謂此為成王之詩也。盖周家以農事開國，故周公告成王，其見于詩有若《七月》，其見于書有若《無逸》，欲其知稼穡之艱難與小人之依也。厥後宣王不藉千畝，而虢公諫之。於乎！觀虢公之所以諫，則知周公之所以憂矣。

translation_en:
…the proper season—what more could one seek? Those newly opened fields have only just been established and are difficult to work: what should be done now? Do not call them difficult and therefore work them carelessly. The older fields are already well cultivated and easy to work: what should be done now? Do not call them easy and therefore work them negligently. It was Heaven that bestowed wheat and barley upon us, commanding that all should be nourished. Now the wheat-harvest season is approaching. When the farmers bring in the wheat, they can receive the splendid bounty of the Lord on High. May we discern an auspicious sign for the year? When well-being descends from Heaven, the abundant harvest is plentiful indeed. Thus the year's grain ripens, and the farmers bring it in; Heaven will again grant a plentiful harvest to our newer and older fields. May we have hope for the year? The proper season is easily missed, so one must be diligent; results readily become apparent, so one must exert oneself. With such concern for agriculture, the king of Zhou may indeed be said to have understood the urgency of attending to the foremost task.
Commentators say that this is a poem of King Cheng's time. The house of Zhou founded its state upon agriculture. Thus, among the Duke of Zhou's admonitions to King Cheng, those appearing in the Book of Odes include “The Seventh Month,” and those appearing in the Book of Documents include “Against Idleness.” He wished the king to understand the hardships of sowing and reaping and what the common people depended upon for their livelihood. Later, King Xuan failed to perform the ritual plowing of the thousand-mu field, and the Duke of Guo remonstrated with him. Alas! Observing why the Duke of Guo remonstrated, we understand why the Duke of Zhou was anxious.
Spring and Autumn Annals
“In summer, in the sixth month, the duke met with the Marquis of Qi, the Duke of Song, the Marquis of Chen, and the Earl of Zheng, and they jointly entered into a covenant at You.” The twenty-seventh year of Duke Zhuang.
Wang Xueyi.

The Spring and Autumn Annals records the wavering state's participation in a common covenant, showing how fully the hegemonic state had won the allegiance of the others. Why is this so? The many cannot be forced into unanimity, yet the covenant at You achieved it. This is why the Sage recorded it specially, conveying his approval of Duke Huan. Now, at the covenant at You, only four states followed Qi. Why, then, does the Spring and Autumn Annals call it a “common” covenant? Because the feudal lords all gave him their allegiance. How do we know this? Because the Earl of Zheng shared their purpose.
Now, it is human nature to turn away when suspicious and to withhold wholehearted commitment when divided in allegiance: neither amounts to sharing a common purpose. From the meeting at Beixing, Qi gained the adherence of the feudal lords, but they remained suspicious, saying: “How do we know that he is not drawing the feudal lords along to pursue his private ends?” At that time, however, Duke Huan, concerned that the Chinese states were being tainted by barbarian ways, led men through the great principles of righteousness. His capacity to secure the Chinese states and repel the barbarians became more apparent each day. Those feudal lords had all suffered at the hands of the barbarians. How could they fail to welcome him and come together to give him their allegiance?
After the two meetings at Juan, Zheng entered into covenant with Qi, but afterward again wavered in its allegiance, saying: “How do we know that he is not using the Son of Heaven to magnify himself?” At that time, however, Duke Huan, concerned at the deficiencies of the Zhou royal house, punished Jing-Chu, and his formidable power became more manifest each day. The Earl of Zheng had secretly sided with Chu. How could he fail to fear Duke Huan, reverse his course, and follow him once more? 非反覆也。由是而驅之南歟，則陘亭、召陵，楚人挫矣。三十年經營之謀，此役居多。論其事，雖侯伯之專，而其實振王靈之微，視他盟為何如哉？即諸侯之同以占伯業，盖近悅遠來，勢非勉強也。由是而帥之西歟，則首止、葵丘，王室尊矣。九合一匡之績，兹盟為兆。據其跡，雖牲歃之煩，而其實乃衣裳之會，視他盟不猶愈乎？故《春秋》於斯盟而特書曰「同」，所以著鄭伯之志而見諸侯之輯爾。《穀梁》子所謂「授之諸侯」是也。予桓之意深矣！嗚呼！五侯九伯之霸遠矣。宰孔賜胙，天命勞加，是役也。俾在北杏創伯之前，則小白伐楚尊周功烈，當於方叔、仲山甫輩論矣。惜乎桓公君臣智不足以語此！

translation_en:
…was not fickle. If he then drove them south, the men of Chu would be checked at Xingting and Shaoling. Of the plans pursued over thirty years, this undertaking accounted for a great part of their success. Judged by the deed, it was indeed the unilateral action of a leader of the feudal lords; in substance, however, it revived the waning majesty of the king. How did it compare with other covenants? From the unity of the feudal lords one could divine the prospects of his hegemony: those nearby rejoiced and those far away came to him; their convergence was not forced. If he then led them west, the royal house would be honored at Shouzhi and Kuiqiu. The achievement of assembling the lords nine times and setting the realm right was foreshadowed by this covenant. Judged by its outward forms, it involved the cumbersome rites of sacrificial victims and blood oaths; in substance, however, it was a peaceful assembly in ceremonial robes. Was it not superior to other covenants?
Thus, for this covenant the Spring and Autumn Annals specifically records the word “together,” thereby revealing the intention of the Earl of Zheng and showing the concord of the feudal lords. This is what Master Guliang meant by “entrusting him with the feudal lords.” Profound indeed is the intention to accord approval to Duke Huan! Alas, the hegemony exercised over the five ranks of lords and the chiefs of the nine regions lay far in the past [?]. Minister Kong bestowed sacrificial meat, and the royal command conferred commendation: such was this undertaking. Had it occurred before the founding of the hegemony at Beixing, Xiaobai’s achievements in campaigning against Chu and honoring Zhou would deserve discussion alongside those of Fang Shu and Zhongshan Fu. Regrettably, Duke Huan and his ministers lacked the wisdom to comprehend this!
“The men of Chu extinguished Shu and Liao.” 〔Eighth year of Duke Xuan〕
Liu Cai

春秋志外患有可憂，示內治不可忽也。觀舒蓼之滅，特志于經，聖人經世之慮遠矣。且楚本南夷，天下莫强。我宣中葉，憑陵尤甚：窺周輙敢於問鼎，而不王之心已著；爭鄭屢至於加兵，而圖伯之勢方張。廼今莊也，滅舒蓼而疆滑汭，勢益以强，匪直為小醜之患；盟吳越而騷江漢，志益以驕，有事為大邦之仇。此夷夏盛衰之機，世道升降之會也。經斯世者，其若之何？盖必恐懼省戒，未雨而訂桑土之謀，所以治內者益慎；經營圖回，未濟而謹衣袽之備，所以防外者益嚴。曰安曰攘，義無不著，而膺懲之訓不可隳也；否則，冠裳之變，誰其弭之？或奇或正，慮無不周，而戰守之策所宜講也；否則，門庭之寇，胡以禦之？噫！陘亭次而寔征之命修，昔之匡合者然也。于時諸侯有能奮然而振其烈者乎？城濮戰而捍難之勛繼，昔之攘斥者然也。于時諸侯有能惕然而修其職者乎？是故聖人致望中國之意有如
translation_en:
Examiner Zhang, Grand Secretary, comments: “Concise and rigorous.”

The Spring and Autumn Annals records external dangers that give cause for concern, showing that internal government must not be neglected. Consider how the destruction of Shu and Liao is expressly recorded in the Classic: far-reaching indeed was the sage’s concern for ordering the world. Chu was originally a state of the southern barbarians, yet none under Heaven was stronger. In the middle years of our Duke Xuan’s reign, its encroachments became especially severe. Casting covetous eyes upon Zhou, it dared to inquire about the tripods, already revealing its intention not to acknowledge the king. Repeatedly resorting to arms in its contest for Zheng, it was steadily gaining the power to seek hegemony. Now King Zhuang destroyed Shu and Liao and extended his boundaries to Huarui. His power grew still greater: this was no mere menace from a petty adversary. He made covenants with Wu and Yue and disturbed the lands of the Jiang and Han rivers. His ambitions grew still more arrogant; in the event of hostilities, he would be an enemy of the great states. This was a critical juncture in the relative fortunes of the barbarians and the Xia, a turning point in the rise or decline of order in the world. What should those responsible for governing such an age have done?

Surely they should have examined and admonished themselves in fear, planning to secure the nest with mulberry roots before the rain came, and thus exercising still greater care in internal government. They should have planned and contrived, carefully preparing rags to stop leaks before crossing the water, and thus making their defenses against external threats still more rigorous. Whether securing peace within or repelling enemies without, they must make every duty manifest; the injunction to strike and punish must not be abandoned. Otherwise, who could avert the transformation of our civilization’s caps and robes into barbarian dress? Whether employing unexpected or conventional tactics, they must consider every contingency and give proper attention to strategies for battle and defense. Otherwise, how could they repel invaders at their very gates?

Alas! When the army encamped at Xing, the mandate to conduct punitive expeditions was renewed: such was the achievement of the former leader who set the realm right and united the lords. Among the feudal lords of this later time, was there anyone who could rouse himself and revive that achievement? When the battle was fought at Chengpu, the meritorious work of warding off calamity was carried forward: such was the achievement of the former leader who drove back the barbarians. Among the feudal lords of this later time, was there anyone who could become vigilant and fulfill his duties? Thus the sage’s hopes for the central states were such as…

translation_en:
…such was the sage’s hope for the central states. Otherwise, when barbarians attacked one another, the rules did not call for recording it. Why, then, was this particular event recorded? At this time, Duke Cheng of Jin was weak, while King Zhuang of Chu rose to ascendancy in his stead. Since conquering Yong, he had not passed a day without contemplating expansion northward. That he had not yet fully realized his ambitions was presumably because he thought that our Xia states still had capable men. Subsequently, however, he entered Chen, besieged Zheng, defeated Jin, and destroyed Xiao, flaunting his military might to intimidate the central states. Yet no one ultimately arose to restrain him. Alas! Here one can discern the changes in the condition of the age.
Book of Rites
“When standing, bend like a chime stone and let the pendant ornaments hang down. When the lord’s pendants rest against his body, the minister’s should hang down; when the lord’s pendants hang down, the minister’s should trail on the ground.”
He Tao
Associate Examiner Wang, Supervising Secretary, comments: “Fully develops the meaning of a minister’s reverence for his lord.”
Associate Examiner Gong, Senior Compiler, comments: “Grasps the purport of the ritual classic.”
Examiner Huo, Academician, comments: “Antique and plain.”
Examiner Zhang, Grand Secretary, comments: “The meaning is fully expressed.”
In discussing the reverence expressed by one’s standing posture, one should take the lord’s posture as the measure and show still greater reverence. Reverence is the foundation of ritual practice. How much more, when a minister performs rites with his lord, must he observe the lord and increase his own reverence accordingly! The recorder of rites presumably meant that nothing in ritual is more important than distinctions of rank, and no distinction is more stringent than that between lord and minister. Thus, in standing, one must make one’s inferior position distinct [?], without flattery: this is the constant rule of ritual. As for holding a superior’s ritual vessels or bearing ceremonial silk and a jade tablet…

辟則有君臣之禮焉有上下之交焉故其立也
以身則磬折卑之而不敢高也以佩則垂俯之
而不敢仰也夫磬折垂佩固禮之節也若主佩
垂而臣佩亦垂不幾於君臣之無別乎上下之
無辨乎故主佩倚於身焉則臣當垂佩也主佩
垂焉則臣又當委佩於地也一高卑之間君無

辟，則有君臣之禮焉，有上下之交焉。故其立也，以身則磬折，卑之而不敢高也；以佩則垂，俯之而不敢仰也。夫磬折垂佩，固禮之節也。若主佩垂而臣佩亦垂，不幾於君臣之無別乎？上下之無辨乎？故主佩倚於身焉，則臣當垂佩也；主佩垂焉，則臣又當委佩於地也。一高卑之間，君無驕而臣無諂；俯仰之頃，上不偪而下不僭。禮道則然也。抑聖人制禮，本於天而殽於地者也。故曰：「天尊地卑，君臣定矣。」周衰，下堂而見諸侯者，不以為辱；拜乎上者，不以為泰。所以然者，特由禮教之不明耳。夫禮也者，聖人馭世之大坊，宜記者於此詳焉。

此四者，心之莫同也。知其心，然後能救其失也。教也者，長善而救其失者也。

郭宗臯

translation_en:
…bi jade discs [?]: here there are the rites governing ruler and minister and the interactions between superior and subordinate. Thus, when standing, one bends the body like a chime stone, lowering it and not daring to stand tall; one lets the pendant jades hang down, inclining forward and not daring to lean back. Bending like a chime stone and letting the pendants hang are indeed prescribed observances of ritual. Yet if the ruler’s pendants hang down and the minister’s also hang down, would this not verge on effacing the distinction between ruler and minister, leaving superior and subordinate undifferentiated? Therefore, when the ruler’s pendants rest against his body, the minister should let his hang down; when the ruler’s hang down, the minister should let his reach the ground. In these differences of height, the ruler shows no arrogance and the minister no flattery; in these movements of bowing and straightening, the superior does not impose unduly, and the subordinate does not overstep his station. Such is the way of ritual. Moreover, when the sages established ritual, they grounded it in Heaven and patterned it upon Earth. Thus it is said: “Heaven is exalted and Earth is lowly; the positions of ruler and minister are thereby determined.” In the decline of the Zhou, those who descended from the hall to receive the feudal lords did not consider it humiliating, while those who bowed above the steps did not consider it presumptuous. This happened solely because the teaching of ritual was no longer clearly understood. Ritual is the great bulwark by which the sages govern the world; it is fitting that the recorder should treat this matter in detail.

“These four arise from differences of mind. Only after understanding their minds can one remedy their failings. Teaching means nurturing what is good and remedying their failings.”

Guo Zonggao.

Associate Examiner Gong, Senior Compiler, comments: “Balanced and mild; worthy of recitation.”
Examiner Huo, Academician, comments: “Even and coherent.”

學者之失當知，教者之責斯盡。夫未有不知人之心而能教人者也，此學者之失，教者所宜必知也歟！且夫人之為心不同，學之所失頓異，然欲反其同而變其異，不在於知其心乎？知其失之多者，從而裒之；失之寡者，從而益之：庶多不為夸，寡不為隘也。失之易者，從而退之；失之止者，從而進之：庶易不以驕，止不以阻也。夫所貴於教者，以能長善而成人之美也，以能救失，不成人之惡也。長人之善，則德日崇；其循循之誘，蓋因材而篤之，不知其人之心可乎？救人之失，則義日徙；其諄諄之誨，蓋因病而藥之，不知其人之心可乎？苟使學者之失，教者有所不知焉，則此為強聒，彼為徒聞而已，夫何益哉？抑考善教者，莫如孔子。如子貢多學而識，宰我信道不篤，子路之兼人，冉求之自畫，雖孔門弟子，亦不能無所失者。然卒能以言語、政事列之四科，而為天下之英才焉，則知夫子之教真能知人之
translation_en:
Examiner, Grand Secretary Zhang, comments: “Refined and essential.”

The faults of learners must be understood; only then is the teacher’s responsibility fully discharged. No one has ever been able to teach others without understanding their minds. Surely, then, learners’ faults are something teachers must understand! People differ in their minds, and their errors in learning differ markedly. Yet, if one wishes to restore their common ground and transform their differences, does this not depend on understanding their minds? When one recognizes that their fault lies in excessive learning, one should reduce it; when their fault lies in insufficient learning, one should increase it. Thus, abundance may avoid becoming ostentation, and scantiness may avoid becoming narrowness. When their fault lies in taking learning too lightly, one should restrain them; when it lies in stopping short, one should urge them forward. Thus, ease may not lead to arrogance, nor stopping short to obstruction.

What makes teaching valuable is its ability to nurture goodness and bring people’s admirable qualities to fulfillment, and its ability to remedy faults without bringing their bad qualities to fulfillment. Nurturing people’s goodness makes their virtue grow daily. Such orderly guidance strengthens them according to their capacities: could this be done without understanding their minds? Remedying people’s faults enables them to advance daily in righteousness. Such earnest instruction prescribes remedies according to their ailments: could this be done without understanding their minds? If there are faults in learners that their teachers do not understand, then the teachers merely harangue them, while the learners merely hear to no purpose. What benefit could there be?

Now, among those skilled in teaching, none compares with Confucius. That by which the sage unifies all activity under Heaven is stillness alone. What is stillness? It is the original substance of human nature, that by which human beings are human. Since all are equally human, all equally possess this nature; why, then, must they await the sage? Human beings are still at birth: this is their Heaven-endowed nature. Affected by external things, they become active: these are the desires of that nature. It is precisely through being stirred by desire that the stillness of their nature becomes obscured. The obscuring of stillness necessarily comes through activity; the unification of activity necessarily comes through stillness. title: 嘉靖八年會試錄
text:
立極焉而後得謂之人極也極之為言也在夫
人者即其在天者也吾嘗觀之天矣夫動靜者
陰陽之道也上天之載無聲無臭靜之極也故
曰維天之命於穆不已天者人之本也性者天
之則也循理斯靜靜斯天從欲斯動動斯人靜
也者其聖人立極之本乎動也者其斯人不協
于極之由乎嗚呼性之本體日以不明而天下
之動日以不一吉凶悔吝者生乎動者也是故
人逞其私利而習偷擇便之術興焉人逞其私
===
辯而異端曲學之說興焉人逞其私智而澆囂
傾詐之俗興焉人逞其私力而攘奪爭戰之禍
興焉其究也邦家失其理生民失其常萬物失
其紀天地失其位是曷從生哉欲之無厭而動
之不可一也夫如是而後知動之不一之為害
而聖人立極之功不可少於天下是故聖人之
立極也仁其發也義其裁也中其行也正其處
也正義以為體中仁以為用而必曰主靜云者

What is meant by this ultimate standard is that what resides in human beings is precisely what resides in Heaven. I have considered this in observing Heaven. Movement and stillness are the Way of yin and yang. The workings of Heaven above have neither sound nor scent: this is the utmost stillness. Thus it is said: “Heaven’s mandate—ah, how profound and unceasing!” Heaven is the root of humanity; human nature is Heaven’s rule. Following principle brings stillness, and stillness accords with Heaven; following desire brings movement, and movement belongs to the human. Is not stillness the foundation upon which the sage establishes the ultimate standard? Is not movement the reason people fail to accord with that standard? Alas! The original substance of human nature grows ever more obscure, while the movements of the world grow ever less unified. Good fortune, misfortune, regret, and humiliation arise from movement. Thus, when people indulge their private interests, techniques of taking easy shortcuts and choosing expedient courses arise; when they indulge their private disputations, doctrines of heterodoxy and distorted learning arise; when they indulge their private cleverness, customs of frivolity, clamorous contention, manipulation, and deceit arise; when they indulge their private strength, the calamities of plunder, strife, and warfare arise. In the end, states and households lose their proper order, the people lose their constant norms, the myriad things lose their organizing principles, and Heaven and Earth lose their proper places. text:
者性之德也動亦靜靜亦靜合外内之道也譬
則元亨利貞之運於於穆之天也於此見聖人
全動靜之德而常本之於靜此人極之所以立
也衆人具動靜之理而常失之於動此人極之
所以不立也修此者君子者也動而吉者也悖
此者小人者也動而凶者也時而修焉時而悖
焉動而悔吝者也夫人固安能無動哉惟其無
從欲而動焉而何惡於動是其動也乃所以為
靜也故其靜非寂也其動非妄也而天下之動
===
於是乎可一矣性之於人大矣哉縱之從欲而
潰决横流也將無不至焉反之於靜而合乎天
也將無不至焉是故聖人以此立極所以成位
乎中天地日月四時鬼神莫之能違也而况於
人乎後周子而言靜者外性而言者也斯其靜
也乃所以為動而又奚動之可一哉欲協于聖
人之極者深辨乎此焉可也

translation_en:
…are virtues of human nature. In activity there is stillness, and in stillness there is stillness: this is the Way that unites the outward and the inward. It is like the operation of origination, prevalence, benefit, and constancy in august Heaven. Here we see that the sage fully embodies the virtues of activity and stillness, yet always roots them in stillness. This is how the ultimate standard for humanity is established. Ordinary people possess the principles of activity and stillness, yet constantly go astray in activity. This is why the ultimate standard for humanity is not established among them. Those who cultivate this are noble persons, whose actions bring good fortune; those who go against it are petty persons, whose actions bring misfortune. Those who sometimes cultivate it and sometimes go against it incur regret and humiliation through their actions. How, indeed, could people be without activity? Provided that they do not act in pursuit of desires, what is objectionable about activity? Such activity itself constitutes stillness. Thus their stillness is not mere quiescence, and their activity is not wayward; through this, all activity under Heaven can be brought into unity.

How great is the significance of human nature for humankind! If one lets it follow desires, it bursts its banks and floods unchecked: there is no extreme to which it will not go. If one returns it to stillness and brings it into accord with Heaven, there is no height it cannot attain. Thus the sage establishes the ultimate standard through this, thereby taking his proper place at the center. Heaven and Earth, the sun and moon, the four seasons, and ghosts and spirits cannot depart from it—how much less can human beings! Those who have spoken of stillness after Master Zhou have spoken of it apart from human nature. Their stillness thus gives rise to activity; how, then, could activity be brought into unity? Those who wish to accord with the sage’s ultimate standard should make a searching distinction on this point.

text:

聖人之制禮也法天之經也正地之紀也
定人之倫也盡物之制也以建天下國家

制盡而後物曲可利也倫定而後人官可
