translation_en:
Associate Examiner Liao, Right Mentor, comments: “Governing a state through ritual: you may be said to understand its essentials.”
Examiner Huo, Academician, comments: “He understands the sources and ramifications; his writing also has vigor.”
Examiner Zhang, Grand Secretary, comments: “A scholar who understands ritual.”
When the sages established ritual, they took Heaven’s constant patterns as their model, set Earth’s ordering principles aright, fixed human relationships, and fully prescribed the proper regulation of things, thereby establishing the ultimate standard for all under Heaven, the states, and the families. Thus, only after this standard is established can all under Heaven, the states, and the families be governed; only after regulations are complete can things be put to beneficial use in all their particulars; only after relationships are fixed can people fulfill their functions; only after the ordering principles are set aright can the features of the land be suitably employed; and only after Heaven’s constant patterns are taken as the model does the Way of Heaven prevail. Hence it is said: “Ritual is rooted in Heaven, takes Earth as its pattern, is arrayed in relation to ghosts and spirits, and extends to mourning and sacrifice, archery and charioteering, capping and marriage, and court audiences and diplomatic visits.” Therefore the sages attached great importance to ritual.
Confucius said: “I can speak of the rites of Xia, but Qi provides insufficient corroboration. I can speak of the rites of Yin, but Song provides insufficient corroboration.” He also said: “Zhou looked to the two preceding dynasties. How splendid its cultural forms! I follow Zhou.” Thus, when the Duke of Zhou established ritual, he modeled it on Heaven’s constant patterns, set Earth’s ordering principles aright, fixed human relationships, and fully prescribed regulations, thereby providing the people with an ultimate standard.
In the Rites of Zhou, the auspicious rites include sacrifices with ascending smoke, offerings burned on a pyre, the burning of piled firewood, blood sacrifices, burial and immersion of offerings, the dismemberment of sacrificial victims, the presentation of portions of victims and libations, offerings of food, and the seasonal sacrifices called ci, yue, chang, and zheng. The inauspicious rites include mourning, rites for famine and for offering condolences, and rites for giving assistance and relief. The guest rites include spring and summer court audiences, autumn audiences and occasional meetings, and assemblies…

title: 嘉靖八年會試錄
text:
同問視也軍禮則有若師也均之與田役
之與封也嘉禮則有若飲食也婚冠也賓
射饗燕也脤膰之於賀慶也斯禮也建諸
天地質諸鬼神所以教天下後世之為人
上者也其在儀禮嘉禮則有若士冠也士
婚也公食大夫有司徹也鄉飲鄉射也賓
禮則有若覲也聘也凶禮則有若喪服也
士喪也士虞既夕也斯禮也通于上下宜
于臣民所以教天下後世之為人下者也
===
是故凡屬乎郊禋而順時則象者明天道
也故曰法天之經也凡屬乎社稷而體國
經野者明地道也故曰正地之紀也凡屬
乎宗廟朝廷而行於天下者明人道也故
曰定人之倫也凡屬乎天之所生地之所
化人情之可以義起而曲成不遺者明物
理也故曰盡物之制也夫周禮之為禮也
其體至大而不窮而周官一篇則周禮之
綱領也儀禮之為禮也其用至周而無間

punctuated:
同、問、視也。軍禮則有若師也，均之與田，役之與封也。嘉禮則有若飲食也，婚冠也，賓射饗燕也，脤膰之於賀慶也。斯禮也，建諸天地，質諸鬼神，所以教天下後世之為人上者也。其在《儀禮》，嘉禮則有若士冠也，士婚也，公食大夫、有司徹也，鄉飲、鄉射也。賓禮則有若覲也，聘也。凶禮則有若喪服也，士喪也，士虞、既夕也。斯禮也，通于上下，宜于臣民，所以教天下後世之為人下者也。
是故凡屬乎郊禋而順時則象者，明天道也，故曰法天之經也。凡屬乎社稷而體國經野者，明地道也，故曰正地之紀也。凡屬乎宗廟朝廷而行於天下者，明人道也，故曰定人之倫也。凡屬乎天之所生、地之所化、人情之可以義起而曲成不遺者，明物理也，故曰盡物之制也。
夫《周禮》之為禮也，其體至大而不窮，而《周官》一篇則《周禮》之綱領也。《儀禮》之為禮也，其用至周而無間。

…assemblies, inquiries, and visits. Military rites include the mustering of armies, equalizing burdens, hunting, mobilizing labor, and establishing boundaries. Auspicious rites include eating and drinking, weddings and cappings, guest archery, ceremonial feasts and banquets, gifts of sacrificial meat, and congratulations and celebrations. These rites are established upon Heaven and Earth and verified before ghosts and spirits; they instruct those throughout the world and in later generations who occupy positions above others. In the Ceremonies and Rites (Yili), auspicious rites include the Capping of a Gentleman, the Marriage of a Gentleman, a Ruler’s Formal Meal for a Grand Master, the Officers’ Removal of the Offerings, District Drinking, and District Archery. Guest rites include Audiences and Diplomatic Visits. Mourning rites include Mourning Garments, the Funeral of a Gentleman, the Repose Sacrifice for a Gentleman, and the Evening before Burial. These rites apply to both higher and lower ranks and are appropriate to subjects and common people; they instruct those throughout the world and in later generations who occupy positions below others.
Thus, everything pertaining to suburban sacrifices and pure offerings that follows the seasons and takes celestial phenomena as its model makes clear the Way of Heaven. Hence the saying, “Model oneself on Heaven’s constant principles.” Everything pertaining to the altars of soil and grain that lays out the capital and demarcates the countryside makes clear the Way of Earth. Hence the saying, “Set right Earth’s ordering.” Everything pertaining to ancestral temples and the court that is practiced throughout the world makes clear the Way of humanity. Hence the saying, “Establish human relationships.” Everything pertaining to what Heaven produces and Earth transforms, and to what may be instituted in accordance with righteousness on the basis of human feelings, bringing each particular to fulfillment without omission, makes clear the principles of things. Hence the saying, “Fully establish the regulations for all things.”
As a system of rites, the Rites of Zhou (Zhouli) has a structure of the utmost breadth, inexhaustible in its scope; the chapter “Offices of Zhou” (Zhouguan) supplies its guiding outline. As a system of rites, the Ceremonies and Rites is utterly comprehensive in its application, leaving no gaps…

text:
而曲禮諸篇則儀禮之類例也夫周禮體
大而不窮則可以兼其全而大司徒之五
典大司馬之九伐吉禮軍禮具載也儀禮

之戒百官亦未為無吉禮軍禮也宋儒朱
熹慨王安石廢古儀禮棄經任傳乃欲取
儀禮為經禮記為傳以復周公制禮之舊

太祖高皇帝稽古禮文法周為治宏綱大要舉
之于上以正百官者蓋取諸周禮繁文縟
節頒之于下以正萬民者蓋取諸儀禮攷

考夫澄之所咎者唐儒亡禮之罪也熹之
所慨者宋臣廢禮之罪也亡禮之罪小廢
禮之罪大君子不能無憾焉爾矣哉
太祖高皇帝稽古禮文法周為治宏綱大要舉
之于上以正百官者盖取諸周禮繁文縟
節頒之于下以正萬民者盖取諸儀禮致
之洪武初年
儒臣陶安定
punctuated:
而《曲禮》諸篇則《儀禮》之類例也。夫《周禮》體大而不窮，則可以兼其全，而大司徒之五典、大司馬之九伐，吉禮、軍禮具載也。《儀禮》用周而無間，而《少牢饋食》之宿尸、《大射儀》之戒百官，亦未為無吉禮、軍禮也。宋儒朱熹慨王安石廢古《儀禮》，棄經任傳，乃欲取《儀禮》為經、《禮記》為傳，以復周公制禮之舊，而其徒黃榦、楊復又編為《集解》以發明之。至元儒吳澄考定三禮，附以《公符》《盛德》諸篇為《儀禮》逸經，而歸咎于唐初諸儒之失考。夫澄之所咎者，唐儒亡禮之罪也；熹之所慨者，宋臣廢禮之罪也。亡禮之罪小，廢禮之罪大，君子不能無憾焉爾矣。
我太祖高皇帝稽古禮文，法周為治。宏綱大要，舉之于上以正百官者，蓋取諸《周禮》；繁文縟節，頒之于下以正萬民者，蓋取諸《儀禮》。攷之洪武初年，命儒臣陶安定
translation_en:
…while the chapters entitled “Summary of Ritual” (Quli) and others provide the categories and precedents of the Ceremonies and Rites (Yili). The Rites of Zhou (Zhouli), being vast and inexhaustible in its scope, can encompass the whole: the five teachings of the Minister of Education and the nine grounds for punitive campaigns of the Minister of War are recorded in it, with both sacrificial and military rites fully represented. The Ceremonies and Rites is comprehensive and without gaps in its applications; its notification of the impersonator of the deceased in “The Offering of Food with a Lesser Sacrificial Victim” and its admonition to the assembled officials in “The Ceremony of the Great Archery Contest” likewise show that it is not without sacrificial and military rites.
The Song scholar Zhu Xi lamented that Wang Anshi had discarded the ancient Ceremonies and Rites, abandoning the classic and relying on its commentary. He therefore wished to take the Ceremonies and Rites as the classic and the Record of Rites (Liji) as its commentary, thereby restoring the original ritual institutions of the Duke of Zhou. His disciples Huang Gan and Yang Fu further compiled collected explanations to elucidate them. Later, the Yuan scholar Wu Cheng critically examined and established the texts of the Three Ritual Classics, appending such chapters as “Ducal Tally” (Gongfu) [?] and “Abundant Virtue” (Shengde) as lost canonical texts of the Ceremonies and Rites. He attributed the fault to inadequate investigation by the scholars of the early Tang. What Wu Cheng blamed was the Tang scholars’ culpability for the loss of rites; what Zhu Xi lamented was the Song minister’s culpability for abolishing rites. Culpability for losing rites is lesser; culpability for abolishing them is greater. A gentleman cannot but regret this.
Our Emperor Taizu Gao examined the ritual institutions of antiquity and modeled his government on Zhou. The broad principles and essential provisions instituted at the highest level to regulate the officials were drawn from the Rites of Zhou; the elaborate forms and detailed observances promulgated below to regulate all the people were drawn from the Ceremonies and Rites. Examining the early years of the Hongwu reign, we find that he commanded the scholarly official Tao An to establish…

title: 嘉靖八年會試錄
text:
郊社群祀禮詹同定
四廟袷祭禮李善長定官民喪禮朱升定祭祀
齊戒禮崔亮定五祀禮劉基定百官朝會
禮魏觀定祝祭禮陶凱定軍禮而又招延
俊乂如曾魯徐一夔董彞梁寅輩編集
大明集禮吉禮則有若祀天也祀地也宗廟也
社稷也朝日也夕月也先農也太歲風雲
雷雨也岳鎮海瀆山川城隍也旗纛也馬
祖馬歩馬社也祭厲也祀典神祇也三皇
===
孔子也嘉禮則有若朝會也冊拜也冠也
婚也鄉飲也賓禮則有若朝貢也遣使也
軍禮則有若親征也遣將也大射也凶禮
則有若弔賻也喪儀也斯禮也其六官之
所總者則周禮之遺意也其庶司之所分
者則儀禮之遺意也師其意不泥其文用
其大或畧其細準諸古而有合達之今而
可行所謂法天之經正地之紀定人之倫
盡物之制而為天下國家之極者無所不

translation_en:
…the rites for the suburban sacrifices, the altars of soil, and the various other sacrifices; Zhan Tong established the rites for the joint sacrifice at the four ancestral temples; Li Shanchang established mourning rites for officials and commoners; Zhu Sheng established the rites of fasting and purification for sacrifices; Cui Liang established the rites for the five household sacrifices; Liu Ji established the rites for court assemblies of all officials; Wei Guan established rites for sacrificial invocations; and Tao Kai established military rites. Furthermore, outstanding men such as Zeng Lu, Xu Yikui, Dong Yi, and Liang Yin were invited to compile the Collected Rites of the Great Ming (Da Ming jili).

The auspicious rites included sacrifices to Heaven and Earth; rites at the ancestral temples and the altars of soil and grain; the morning sacrifice to the sun and the evening sacrifice to the moon; sacrifices to the First Farmer; to the Grand Year and the spirits of wind, clouds, thunder, and rain; to the sacred peaks, guardian mountains, seas, great rivers, mountains and waterways, and city gods; to military banners and standards; to the Horse Ancestor, Mabu, and the Horse Altar; offerings to restless spirits; sacrifices to the deities entered in the sacrificial register; and sacrifices to the Three Sovereigns and Confucius. The celebratory rites included court assemblies, investitures, capping ceremonies, marriages, and community drinking ceremonies. The guest rites included tribute audiences and the dispatch of envoys. The military rites included campaigns led by the emperor in person, the dispatch of generals, and the great archery ceremony. The inauspicious rites included condolences, contributions toward funeral expenses, and funeral ceremonies.

In these rites, what the six ministries administered collectively preserved the intent of the Rites of Zhou; what was apportioned among the various offices preserved the intent of the Ceremonies and Rites (Yili). They took that intent as their model without being bound by its wording, adopted its major principles while sometimes omitting its finer details, accorded with antiquity when measured against it, and remained practicable when applied to the present. What is meant by taking Heaven’s constant order as a model, setting right Earth’s ordering principles, establishing human relationships, fully providing the regulations appropriate to all things, and thereby furnishing the highest standard for the world, the state, and the ruling house—in none of these respects did they fail to…

title: 嘉靖八年會試錄
text:
用其極矣是誠為我
朝一代之令典而
聖子神孫所當世守以為家法焉者仰惟
皇上憲章
聖祖建其有極高明配天經以法矣博厚配地
紀以正矣明於人倫倫以定矣察於庶物
制以盡矣然禮有本有文無本不立無文
不行故曰明其義者君也能其事者臣也
不明其義君人不全不能其事為臣不全
===
又曰其數可陳也其義難知也知其數而
敢守之天子之所以治天下也邇者
皇上簡命儒臣纂修
明倫大典是明其義矣是禮之本立矣而又
親灑宸翰勅令重修
大明會典以削其訛以補其畧是知禮之文猶
有未備也是當時之為臣者未能陳其數能
其事者之過也然而周禮儀禮不列于學
官則上焉者道無所於揆下焉者法無所

punctuated: 用其極矣。是誠為我朝一代之令典，而聖子神孫所當世守以為家法焉者。仰惟皇上憲章聖祖，建其有極，高明配天，經以法矣；博厚配地，紀以正矣；明於人倫，倫以定矣；察於庶物，制以盡矣。然禮有本有文，無本不立，無文不行。故曰：「明其義者，君也；能其事者，臣也。不明其義，君人不全；不能其事，為臣不全。」又曰：「其數可陳也，其義難知也。知其數而敢守之，天子之所以治天下也。」邇者皇上簡命儒臣纂修《明倫大典》，是明其義矣，是禮之本立矣。而又親灑宸翰，勅令重修《大明會典》，以削其訛，以補其畧，是知禮之文猶有未備也，是當時之為臣者未能陳其數、能其事者之過也。然而《周禮》《儀禮》不列于學官，則上焉者道無所於揆，下焉者法無所
translation_en:
…fully realizing that ultimate standard. This is truly the authoritative code of our dynasty, which its sagely sons and divine descendants should preserve generation after generation as the ruling house’s law. Reverently considering Your Majesty’s emulation of the Sagely Founder and establishment of the supreme standard: your loftiness and brilliance match Heaven, whose constant principles are thereby followed; your breadth and depth match Earth, whose ordering patterns are thereby set right; you understand human relationships, which are thereby settled; and you discern the myriad things, whose proper regulations are thereby fully realized. Yet ritual has both a foundation and outward forms. Without its foundation it cannot stand; without its forms it cannot be put into practice. Thus it is said: “One who understands its meaning is a ruler; one who can carry out its affairs is a minister. Without understanding its meaning, one cannot fully perform the role of ruler; without being able to carry out its affairs, one cannot fully perform the role of minister.” It is also said: “Its particulars can be set forth, but its meaning is difficult to understand. Knowing its particulars and daring to uphold them is how the Son of Heaven governs the world.”

Recently Your Majesty selected and commissioned Confucian officials to compile the Great Compendium Clarifying Human Relationships (Minglun Dadian). This clarifies ritual’s meaning; this establishes its foundation. Moreover, you personally wielded the imperial brush to command a revision of the Collected Statutes of the Great Ming (Da Ming Huidian), eliminating its errors and supplementing its omissions. This shows your recognition that ritual’s outward forms are still incomplete. This incompleteness is the fault of those serving as ministers at the time, who failed to set forth its particulars and carry out its affairs. title: 嘉靖八年會試錄
text:
於守禮之文雖備也而終未能復先王之
典之舊也故曰大人舉禮樂則天地將為
昭焉愚敢以是為
今日望
第二問
粟應麟
同考試官署員外郎李批老成之見如此
同考試官編修金批深識治體
同考試官修撰王批以守法立說最是
===

考試官學士霍批善含蓄
考試官大學士張批忠愛之言
君人者之安天下也惟其善守法而已矣
守法之道勿安于無為勿喜於有為安於
無為謂之因循喜於有為謂之紛更其以
弊天下均也人君為天下譬若治家理身
然里之人有好華者日取其先人之堂構

Thus it is said: “When the great man puts ritual and music into practice, Heaven and Earth will thereby be illuminated.” I humbly venture to make this my hope for the present reign.

Su Yinglin

The ruler brings peace to All-under-Heaven simply by being adept at upholding established laws. The way to uphold laws is neither to rest content with inaction nor to delight in taking action. title: 嘉靖八年會試錄
text:
歲而弗櫛者謂人曰我歲一櫛不勝其病
子日櫛何也是二人者皆過也室可葺而
完也髮可櫛而理也故夫國家之法一日
弗飭則必有廢墜焉惟修而復之斯已矣
而奚紛更為也漢興蓋三十載文帝以恭
默安天下夫自春秋戰國以至秦項戰爭
久矣而得文帝安集而燠休之豈非幸歟
時則有若賈誼勸以興禮教定經制賈山
勸以修大業成德化惜乎文帝不能用而
===
絳灌諸人不足責也宣帝守漢家制度無
所變更獨與丙魏勵精圖治謹擇守令綜
覈名實信賞必罰中興之盛近古所無也
至於尊外戚任宦官誅大臣究漢弊亦自
有漸謂宣帝不能懲創則可若以此詆其
為基禍之主不亦甚乎宋仁宗承三世盈
成之業守四十年恭儉之規宜可以有為
矣而帝也有見於守成無見於振飭君子
小人之雜進西戎北虜之繹騷殆非可以

punctuated:
歲而弗櫛者，謂人曰：「我歲一櫛，不勝其病，子日櫛何也？」是二人者皆過也。室可葺而完也，髮可櫛而理也。故夫國家之法，一日弗飭，則必有廢墜焉。惟修而復之斯已矣，而奚紛更為也？
漢興蓋三十載，文帝以恭默安天下。夫自春秋戰國以至秦項，戰爭久矣，而得文帝安集而燠休之，豈非幸歟？時則有若賈誼勸以興禮教、定經制，賈山勸以修大業、成德化。惜乎文帝不能用，而絳灌諸人不足責也。
宣帝守漢家制度，無所變更，獨與丙魏勵精圖治，謹擇守令，綜覈名實，信賞必罰，中興之盛，近古所無也。至於尊外戚、任宦官、誅大臣，究漢弊亦自有漸。謂宣帝不能懲創則可，若以此詆其為基禍之主，不亦甚乎？
宋仁宗承三世盈成之業，守四十年恭儉之規，宜可以有為矣。而帝也有見於守成，無見於振飭。君子小人之雜進，西戎北虜之繹騷，殆非可以
translation_en:
…went a whole year without combing his hair and said to someone, “I comb my hair once a year and find the discomfort unbearable. Why do you comb yours every day?” Both these men went too far. A house can be repaired and made sound; hair can be combed and put in order. Thus, if the laws of the state go untended for even a day, some will inevitably fall into neglect. Simply repair and restore them, and that is enough. Why engage in incessant alterations?
Some thirty years after the Han arose, Emperor Wen brought peace to the realm through reverence and quiet restraint. From the Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods down to Qin and Xiang Yu, warfare had continued for a long time. Was it not fortunate that the people then had Emperor Wen to settle them in peace and give them comfort and rest? At that time, Jia Yi urged him to promote ritual instruction and establish enduring institutions, while Jia Shan urged him to cultivate the great imperial enterprise and bring moral transformation to fruition. Alas, Emperor Wen could not put their advice into practice; men such as Jiang and Guan scarcely merit reproach.
Emperor Xuan upheld the institutions of the Han ruling house without altering them. Working with Bing and Wei, he devoted himself energetically to good government: carefully selecting prefects and magistrates, comprehensively examining whether actual performance matched professed duties, reliably granting rewards, and invariably imposing punishments. The flourishing of this restoration had no parallel in the recent past. As for honoring imperial relatives by marriage, employing eunuchs, and executing high ministers, the abuses of the Han, when traced to their origins, likewise developed gradually. One may say that Emperor Xuan failed to take warning and institute corrective measures. But to denounce him on this account as a ruler who laid the foundations of disaster—is that not excessive?
Emperor Renzong of the Song inherited the fully established prosperity achieved over three reigns and maintained a pattern of reverence and frugality for forty years. He should have been able to accomplish something. Yet the emperor understood how to preserve established achievements, but not how to reinvigorate and set things in order. With exemplary and petty men advancing together, and the western Rong and northern enemies causing continual disturbances, these were hardly circumstances that could be…

title: 嘉靖八年會試錄
text:
揖讓而理也時則有若余靖勸以總攬權
綱范仲淹勸以飭邊防抑僥倖惜乎仁宗
不能用而一時朝臣且有忌之者矣神宗
刻意王道上慕唐虞而王安石不能引進
忠賢廣集羣策驟行新法以擾其民安石
之過也靖康之禍固亦有由而神宗則不
可謂無志者志既不終而又使之蒙釀亂
之名豈其然乎夫是四君者其於守成之
道盖互有得失焉然其君道之優劣固有
===
定論而不可昧也洪惟我
太祖
太宗聖神相繼統天立極創造締構盖五十餘
年之勤典則具存至精至當過漢宋遠甚
所宜千萬年世守勿失者夫復何言顧惟
熈洽之久玩愒之餘安能無廢墜而當修
復之者乎修復之與紛更疑似之間要在
辨之而已毫釐之差千里之謬也今豈無
有假修復之說以濟其紛更者乎亦豈無

punctuated:
揖讓而理也。時則有若余靖勸以總攬權綱，范仲淹勸以飭邊防、抑僥倖，惜乎仁宗不能用，而一時朝臣且有忌之者矣。神宗刻意王道，上慕唐虞，而王安石不能引進忠賢，廣集羣策，驟行新法以擾其民，安石之過也。靖康之禍固亦有由，而神宗則不可謂無志者。志既不終，而又使之蒙釀亂之名，豈其然乎？夫是四君者，其於守成之道，盖互有得失焉。然其君道之優劣，固有定論而不可昧也。
洪惟我太祖、太宗，聖神相繼，統天立極，創造締構，盖五十餘年之勤。典則具存，至精至當，過漢宋遠甚，所宜千萬年世守勿失者，夫復何言？顧惟熈洽之久，玩愒之餘，安能無廢墜而當修復之者乎？修復之與紛更，疑似之間，要在辨之而已。毫釐之差，千里之謬也。今豈無有假修復之說以濟其紛更者乎？亦豈無
translation_en:
…be brought to order through ceremonial deference alone. At that time, men such as Yu Jing urged him to take full command of the essential powers of government, while Fan Zhongyan urged him to strengthen frontier defenses and curb the pursuit of undeserved advantage. Alas, Renzong could not put their advice into practice, and some ministers at court even resented them. Shenzong earnestly aspired to the Kingly Way, looking back in admiration to the ages of Tang Yao and Yu Shun. Yet Wang Anshi failed to bring forward loyal and worthy men and draw widely upon their counsel; instead, he hastily implemented the New Policies, disturbing the people. This was Wang Anshi’s fault. The Jingkang disaster certainly had its causes, but Shenzong cannot be said to have lacked aspiration. His aspiration remained unfulfilled; should he then also be made to bear the reputation of having fomented disorder? How could that be right? These four rulers each had their successes and failures in preserving an inherited achievement. Yet there are settled judgments on their relative merits as rulers, which must not be obscured.
We reverently reflect upon our Taizu and Taizong, sages of divine wisdom succeeding one another, who ruled in accordance with Heaven and established the supreme standard. Their founding and construction of the dynasty entailed more than fifty years of toil. Their statutes and standards remain fully preserved, supremely refined and fitting, far surpassing those of the Han and Song. They should be upheld from generation to generation for countless ages without being lost: what more need be said? Yet after so long a period of peace and harmony, and the complacency and idleness it has fostered, how could there be nothing that has fallen into disuse and requires restoration? Restoration and indiscriminate alteration can appear deceptively similar; the essential task is simply to distinguish them. A discrepancy of a hair’s breadth leads to an error of a thousand li. Are there not people today who invoke restoration as a pretext to carry out their indiscriminate alterations? And are there not also…

title: 嘉靖八年會試錄
text:
有避紛更之嫌以忘其修復者乎疑似之
難辨私智害之也事之源委誠不可以不
究者如使去其私智而行其所無事則智
亦大矣書曰有典有則貽厥子孫詩曰不
愆不忘率由舊章詩書之訓夫人皆知之
而不能守者私智害之也宋儒羅從彥有
曰祖宗德澤不可恃法度不可廢由是觀
之能守
祖宗之法度自可以綿德澤於無窮矣尚可以
===
他求哉今
聖天子在上以恭己之資躬勵精之實興道致
治千載一時若夫
今日天下之事所宜修復而不在於紛更者
惟
聖明擬議以成其變化固自有得之者也則漢
宋之事又奚足多論哉
第三問
王崇

===
他求哉今
聖天子在上以恭己之資躬勵精之實與道致
治千載一時若夫
今日天下之事所宜修復而不在於紛更者
惟
聖明擬議以成其變化固自有得之者也則漢
宋之事又奚足多論哉
第三問　　　　　　王崇
punctuated:
有避紛更之嫌以忘其修復者乎？疑似之難辨，私智害之也。事之源委，誠不可以不究者。如使去其私智而行其所無事，則智亦大矣。《書》曰：「有典有則，貽厥子孫。」《詩》曰：「不愆不忘，率由舊章。」《詩》《書》之訓，夫人皆知之，而不能守者，私智害之也。宋儒羅從彥有曰：「祖宗德澤不可恃，法度不可廢。」由是觀之，能守祖宗之法度，自可以綿德澤於無窮矣，尚可以他求哉？今聖天子在上，以恭己之資，躬勵精之實，興道致治，千載一時。若夫今日天下之事，所宜修復而不在於紛更者，惟聖明擬議以成其變化，固自有得之者也。則漢宋之事，又奚足多論哉？

第三問
王崇
translation_en:
…those who, avoiding the suspicion of meddlesome change, neglect restoration? That it is difficult to distinguish between these seemingly similar courses is due to the harm wrought by self-serving cleverness. The origins and ramifications of affairs must indeed be thoroughly investigated. If one could put aside such cleverness and proceed without contrivance, one’s wisdom would truly be great. The Book of Documents says: “There are statutes and rules to be handed down to their descendants.” The Book of Odes says: “Neither transgressing nor forgetting, follow the old institutions.” Everyone knows these teachings of the Odes and Documents; failure to abide by them arises from the harm wrought by self-serving cleverness. The Song Confucian scholar Luo Congyan said: “The beneficence of the ancestors cannot be relied upon; their laws and institutions must not be abandoned.” Viewed in this light, preserving the laws and institutions of the imperial ancestors will of itself perpetuate their beneficence without end. Can one still seek elsewhere?

Now the sage Son of Heaven reigns above us. With a disposition of reverent self-discipline, he personally devotes himself in earnest to diligent government, promoting the Way and bringing about good order—a conjunction encountered once in a thousand years. As for those affairs of the realm today that call for restoration rather than meddlesome change, Your sagacious Majesty, through deliberation that brings their transformations to fruition, surely has your own insight into them. What need, then, is there to discuss the affairs of the Han and Song at length?

Third Question
Wang Chong

Men of talent depend upon how they are nurtured, and still more upon how they nurture themselves. If scholars’ habits become upright only after cultivation, they still depend upon others. But loyalty, generosity, integrity, and uprightness are qualities scholars ought to cultivate themselves. How could these depend upon the encouragement or discouragement of the times? Thus we know that those responsible for the moral order of the age must indeed nurture scholars, while scholars, in their expectations of themselves, must also truly maintain their self-respect. It is fitting that this should engage your concern. Scholars are the guiding standard for the people and those to whom the multitude looks. Once scholars’ habits are upright, upright men rise together, and the strength of the state follows accordingly. Thus, in antiquity, provision for scholars included the establishment of schools, a system of selection and recommendation, and methods of evaluating performance. Nothing surpasses schools in rectifying virtue and fostering talent; nothing surpasses selection and recommendation in recruiting the worthy and advancing the capable; nothing surpasses performance evaluations in requiring actual achievement commensurate with nominal duties. text:
以當時之士業有定習行有定執官有定
守少而習焉久而安焉不見異物而遷焉
治化之隆人才之盛有自來矣我
國家養士取法成周得人為盛顧習尚日久
乃或有不然者姑以明問所及者言之夫
治經術為文章雖為儒者事也使為文而
適於用談經不詭於聖人亦何不可乎若
惟華靡其詞以取悅人之耳目立異說攻
先儒短長是乃喪志之資而奚以經術文
===
章為哉其弊見於前宋伊川憂之而在今
日則亦有然者矣至於士之從人尤不可
不慎三代之士不輕於請謁以有禮為之
防也及禮亡而俗敝於是有自鬻其身者
矣盖不能謹其分守則貴得凌賤而辱其
身不能順於時命則下必援上而屈其志
始之不善而能有以善其終乎其俗成於
當時后山傷之而在今日殆有甚焉矣夫
空言不可以為教徒法不能以自行是數

translation_en:
…thus the scholars of that time had settled practices in their studies, fixed principles in their conduct, and established duties to uphold in office. They learned these in youth and, with long practice, became at ease in them; unfamiliar things did not turn them aside. The flourishing of good government and moral transformation, and the abundance of talented men, had their sources in this. Our dynasty has nurtured scholars on the model of the Zhou and has been outstanding in obtaining worthy men. Yet as customary practices have persisted over time, some have ceased to accord with this ideal. Let me speak provisionally of the matters raised in your discerning question. Studying the classics and composing literary works are indeed the business of Confucian scholars. If their writing serves practical purposes and their discussion of the classics does not depart from the sages, what could be objectionable? But if they merely embellish their language extravagantly to please people's eyes and ears, advance heterodox interpretations, and attack earlier Confucians by disputing their merits and faults, these become means of losing their moral purpose. What use, then, are classical scholarship and literary composition? These abuses appeared under the former Song dynasty and troubled Yichuan [Cheng Yi]; today, too, such things occur.

As for scholars attaching themselves to others, particular caution is essential. Scholars of the Three Dynasties did not lightly seek audiences with the powerful, because ritual propriety served as a restraint. When ritual propriety disappeared and customs deteriorated, men began to sell themselves. If they cannot carefully uphold the duties proper to their station, the eminent can overbear the lowly and humiliate them; if they cannot accept their circumstances and allotted fate, those below will inevitably seek support from those above and compromise their aspirations. If their beginning is unsound, can they bring matters to a good end? This practice became customary in that earlier age and grieved Houshan [Chen Shidao]; today it is probably still worse. 不敢以為然也以為盡由於學校選舉考

未至而守之者有未慎乎吾於是又知浮

translation_en:
…these abuses: can we say that they do not arise from schools, selection for office, and evaluations of officials? I dare not affirm this. Can we say that they arise entirely from schools, selection for office, and evaluations of officials? Nor do I dare affirm this. Might those who lead have fallen short, while those who uphold their principles have exercised insufficient care? Here I further recognize the sources of frivolity and competitive pursuit of advancement. To eradicate these abuses, we need only urgently reverse these tendencies. Thus, if we strengthen fundamentals and substance, frivolity will subside; if we esteem integrity and modest withdrawal, competitive pursuit of advancement will recede. Although those skilled in a contorted literary style [?] have been rejected, those who study diligently and cherish antiquity are still treated as ordinary men. Although those who have sent no letters to the chief councillors have gained advancement, those whose feet reach both doors [?] still rise alongside them. How can this adequately encourage or deter scholars? I therefore believe that leadership has fallen short: this is the responsibility of those above.
Nevertheless, scholars too bear responsibility. Upon each scholar rests responsibility for the cardinal relationships and constant moral principles. His doing good should not depend upon encouragement from others. To act only after being encouraged is already shallow; how much worse to require others to sustain, supervise, and admonish him, yet still fall short! Only by understanding the Way and cultivating oneself, without occupying oneself with empty words, and by adhering to ritual propriety in dealing with others, unmoved by the lure of profit—as Yichuan and Houshan expected of later students and urged in admonishing the degenerate customs of their age—can one make what one cultivates pure and what one upholds correct. Then these two abuses will naturally disappear. Why is it that not everyone lives up to this?

text:
知其無形也則其圖之也不可以不豫圖
之不豫是之曰窮知其無常也則其防之

無窮也則其修之也不可以不嚴修之不
嚴是之曰弛是故嚴而弗弛謹而弗僨豫
而弗窮古之帝王御夷狄之道莫有踰於
此者矣三代而下若漢武帝若唐太宗亦

頓桀黠益甚鳴弦雲中飲馬桑乾信有如

知其無形也，則其圖之也不可以不豫；圖之不豫，是之曰窮。知其無常也，則其防之也不可以不謹；防之不謹，是之曰僨。知其無窮也，則其修之也不可以不嚴；修之不嚴，是之曰弛。是故嚴而弗弛，謹而弗僨，豫而弗窮，古之帝王御夷狄之道，莫有踰於此者矣。
三代而下，若漢武帝，若唐太宗，亦英雄豪傑之主也。漢自高祖困圍白登，冒頓桀黠益甚，鳴弦雲中，飲馬桑乾，信有如《春秋》敗績茅戎之恥矣。武帝赫然振怒，遣衛青出上谷，李廣出鴈門，公孫敖出代，霍去病出隴西，龍城狼望，空無王庭。乃又南開兩粤，西闢五都，于闐大夏，悉建都護，車師鄯善，俱種屯田。其雄才大畧何如者！然攷其内治，表章六經，明大道也；罷黜百家，闢邪說也；行夏之時，正天統也；恤農之耕，重民事也。而又能容汲黯之諫之戇，任霍金之忠之朴，此其所以異於秦也。胡為乎
translation_en:
…Knowing that it has no visible form, one must plan for it in advance; failing to plan in advance is what is called being at an impasse. Knowing that it is unpredictable, one must guard against it carefully; failing to guard carefully is what is called courting disaster. Knowing that it is inexhaustible, one must be rigorous in putting one’s own affairs in order; failing to do so rigorously is what is called laxity. Thus, to be rigorous without laxity, careful without courting disaster, and prepared without reaching an impasse: the ancient emperors and kings had no better way of controlling the foreign peoples.
After the Three Dynasties, rulers such as Emperor Wu of Han and Emperor Taizong of Tang were also men of heroic stature. In the Han, after Gaozu was trapped and besieged at Baideng, Maodun became ever more ruthless and cunning. His bowstrings rang out in Yunzhong, and he watered his horses in the Sanggan River. This was indeed a humiliation like the defeat at the hands of the Mao Rong recorded in the Spring and Autumn Annals. Emperor Wu, blazing with anger, dispatched Wei Qing through Shanggu, Li Guang through Yanmen, Gongsun Ao through Dai, and Huo Qubing through Longxi. Longcheng and Langwang were left empty of royal courts. He then opened up the two Yue territories to the south and the Five Capitals [?] to the west. In Yutian and Daxia he established protectors-general, and in Jushi and Shanshan he established agricultural garrisons. How extraordinary were his heroic talents and grand strategies! Yet consider his internal government: he gave prominence to the Six Classics to illuminate the Great Way; dismissed the Hundred Schools to exclude heterodox doctrines; followed the calendar of the Xia to rectify the succession ordained by Heaven; and showed concern for farmers’ cultivation to give due weight to the people’s affairs. Moreover, he could tolerate the bluntness of Ji An’s remonstrances and entrust responsibilities to the loyal and straightforward Huo and Jin. This was what distinguished him from the Qin. Why, then, was it that…

至初元三年而有珠崖之棄之議蓋賈捐
之之建白于定國之主持而元帝優游之
過亦有不得辭焉者矣唐自高祖借兵突
厥始畢擁衆日强連兵契丹入寇幽并信

translation_en:
…by the third year of Chuyuan, was there a proposal to abandon Zhuya? It arose from Jia Juanzhi’s submission and Yu Dingguo’s support; yet Emperor Yuan, too, could not escape blame for his excessive irresolution.

In the Tang, after Gaozu borrowed troops from the Tujue, Shibi’s forces grew stronger by the day. He joined forces with the Qidan and invaded You and Bing. This indeed bore out the warning conveyed by the meeting with the Rong at Qian in the Spring and Autumn Annals. Taizong alone displayed courage and wisdom, dispatching Li Jing against Jieli, Chai Shao against Tuyuhun, Guo Xiaoke against Duolu, and Hou Junji against Gaochang. Yinshan and Hanhai were all incorporated into the imperial domain. He then campaigned east against Gaoli and west against Yanqi. Linyi and Xinluo sent envoys bearing tribute, while the Zanpu and Wentai came to the frontier to attend court. How great were his achievements in avenging humiliation and eliminating the violent!

Yet consider his domestic government: he reduced labor service and taxes to secure the foundations of the state; investigated ritual and deliberated on music to elevate moral instruction; released prisoners and reduced punishments out of concern for his people’s lives; and promoted worthy men and established schools to strengthen the conduct of scholars. Moreover, he could tolerate the forthright remonstrances of Wei Zheng and entrust affairs to the decisive counsels of Fang and Du. This was what distinguished him from the Sui. Why, then, by the fifth year of Taihe, was there a proposal to abandon Weizhou? Li Deyu had accepted its surrender, and Niu Sengru was jealous of his achievement; yet Wenzong’s weakness also left him unable to decide the matter.

Nevertheless, after the Yuanguang era began, Emperor Wu depleted the resources of the realm and could not escape his regret over Luntai. Toward the end of the Zhenguan era, Taizong gradually failed to sustain his earlier achievements and could not escape, over Liaozuo…

title: 嘉靖八年會試錄
text:
之悔者何也蓋二君雖有開疆闢地之勳
而無帝王經世之學雖有攘夷匡夏之烈
而無聖賢養心之誠宋儒程頤范祖禹論
之詳矣我
太祖高皇帝汛掃胡元戡定羣雄東極玄菟西
抵青海北盡穹廬南窮炎嶠日際月域氷
竈霜螘罔不來王視禹之舞干苗格武王
之慎德夷賓者一矣我
太宗文皇帝天縱神武廓清華夏漠北稽首交
南效順海東獻賔磧西貢珎雕題辮髮碉
房罽服莫敢我膺視商高宗之荆楚畏服
周宣王之淮夷來同者一矣且以交阯言
之永樂初
命張輔統兵討黎季犛拔彼清化扼彼富良藤
江花歩悉為我有乃郡縣其地為一百三
十四而以黃福撫之至宣德間陳氏復叛
楊榮楊士竒以為勞民傷財無益中國遂
棄之不復矣以哈密言之永樂初

translation_en:
…such regret—why was this? Although these two rulers achieved distinction in opening up and extending their territories, they lacked the learning by which true emperors and kings order the world. Although they performed great deeds in repelling outsiders and sustaining the Chinese realm, they lacked the sincerity with which sages and worthies cultivate the mind. The Song Confucian scholars Cheng Yi and Fan Zuyu discussed this in detail.
Our Emperor Taizu Gao swept away the alien Yuan and subdued the contending warlords. His dominion extended east to Xuantu, west to Qinghai, north throughout the lands of felt tents, and south to the hot mountain ranges. From the sun’s horizon and the moon’s domain, from lands of “icy hearths and frost ants” [?], all came to acknowledge him as sovereign. This was just like the submission of the Miao when Yu danced with shield in hand, and the homage of foreign peoples when King Wu attended carefully to his virtue. Our Emperor Taizong Wen possessed heaven-bestowed martial prowess and brought order throughout the Chinese realm. Those north of the desert bowed their heads; Jiaonan pledged obedience; those east of the sea offered submission; and those west of the desert brought precious tribute. Peoples with tattooed foreheads and braided hair, dwelling in stone towers and wearing woollen garments, dared not oppose us. This was just like the fearful submission of Jing and Chu to King Gaozong of Shang, and the coming of the Huai peoples to acknowledge King Xuan of Zhou.
To take Jiaozhi as an example: early in the Yongle reign, Zhang Fu was commanded to lead troops against Li Jili. He captured Qinghua and secured Fuliang; Tengjiang and Huabu both came into our possession. The territory was then organized into 134 prefectural and county jurisdictions, and Huang Fu was charged with pacifying it. During the Xuande reign, the Chen clan rebelled again. Yang Rong and Yang Shiqi considered that the undertaking exhausted the people and wasted resources without benefiting China, so the territory was abandoned and never recovered. As for Hami, early in the Yongle reign…

title: 嘉靖八年會試錄
text:
封元庶孽脫脫為忠順王以鎮其地設罕東
赤斤六衛互相鈐制北縻撒馬兒罕諸虜
西通天方諸夷皮山蒲海悉為我屬由此
入貢者三十一國至弘治間總兵劉寧旋
師之後邊備漸廢陝巴孱弱土魯番強暴
奪我城池擄我人民而遂棄不守矣議者
以為交阯漢唐之故地哈密甘肅之藩籬
不可失也愚嘗論之漢之珠崖即今之廣
東瓊崖州郡也唐之維州即今之四川松
===
茂諸州也交阯古為日南隔嶺隅之外非
如珠崖之故地之比哈密古為伊吾隔敦
煌之外非如維州之故地之比交阯之亂
其來已遠自宋黎桓篡逆而然矣若不得
已而為哈密計宜于肅州諸鎮儲峙糧餉
整理兵馬內治既實而後遣人開示罕東
諸衛及瓦剌小列禿諸夷俾其驅除元惡
克復城池即犒以厚賞予以舊爵況彼之
來寇也挾同諸夷而我疑其心離其黨以

封元庶孽脫脫為忠順王，以鎮其地，設罕東、赤斤六衛，互相鈐制，北縻撒馬兒罕諸虜，西通天方諸夷，皮山、蒲海悉為我屬。由此入貢者三十一國。至弘治間，總兵劉寧旋師之後，邊備漸廢，陝巴孱弱，土魯番強暴，奪我城池，擄我人民，而遂棄不守矣。議者以為交阯漢唐之故地，哈密甘肅之藩籬，不可失也。愚嘗論之：漢之珠崖，即今之廣東瓊崖州郡也；唐之維州，即今之四川松茂諸州也。交阯古為日南，隔嶺隅之外，非如珠崖之故地之比；哈密古為伊吾，隔敦煌之外，非如維州之故地之比。交阯之亂，其來已遠，自宋黎桓篡逆而然矣。

translation_en:
…enfeoffed Tuotuo, a descendant of a secondary branch of the Yuan imperial house, as Prince of Loyal Obedience to hold that territory. Six guards, including Handong and Chijin, were established to keep one another in check. To the north, they maintained loose control over the various barbarians of Samaerhan; to the west, they maintained communications with the foreign peoples of Tianfang. Pishan and Puhai were all subject to us. Thirty-one countries came to offer tribute by this route. During the Hongzhi reign, after Regional Commander Liu Ning withdrew his army, frontier defenses gradually fell into neglect. Shanba was weak, while Tulufan was powerful and violent: it seized our cities and carried off our people. The territory was consequently abandoned and no longer defended. Those discussing the matter hold that Jiaozhi was former territory of the Han and Tang, and that Hami is the protective barrier of Gansu, so neither may be lost. I have ventured to consider the matter as follows: Zhuya under the Han corresponds to the present prefectures and commanderies of Qiong and Ya in Guangdong; Weizhou under the Tang corresponds to the present prefectures of Song and Mao in Sichuan. Jiaozhi was anciently Rinan, lying beyond the mountain ranges, and cannot be compared with former territory such as Zhuya. Hami was anciently Yiwu, lying beyond Dunhuang, and cannot be compared with former territory such as Weizhou. Disorder in Jiaozhi has a long history: it has been so ever since Li Huan’s rebellious usurpation during the Song.
If we have no alternative but to devise a plan for Hami, we should stockpile provisions and military funds at Suzhou and the other garrisons, and put our troops and horses in order. Once our internal administration rests on a firm footing, we should dispatch men to explain our intentions to Handong and the other guards, and to the foreign peoples of Wala and Xiaolietu, inducing them to expel the chief malefactors and recover the cities. We should then reward them generously and grant them their former noble titles. Moreover, when the enemy comes raiding, it brings the other foreign peoples along with it; we should sow doubts in their minds and divide their allies, in order to…

title: 嘉靖八年會試錄
text:
孤其勢故曰先人有奪人之心者此也不
然閉關絕貢發其番文之譎僞返其降人
之誘引以破其奸且彼之藥物農器俱仰
給于我而我絕之久之自窮蹙悔過矣故
曰致人而不致於人者此也不然保境息
民彼若來寇越交河而後嘉峪越嘉峪而

punctuated:
孤其勢，故曰：「先人有奪人之心者」，此也。不然，閉關絕貢，發其番文之譎僞，返其降人之誘引，以破其奸。且彼之藥物、農器俱仰給于我，而我絕之，久之自窮蹙悔過矣。故曰：「致人而不致於人者」，此也。不然，保境息民。彼若來寇，越交河而後嘉峪，越嘉峪而後瓜沙，千里裹糧，師老馬疲；而固我城堡，守我斥堠，斂我頭畜，堅壁清野，待其惰而後擊之。彼不宵遁，必乞降矣。故曰：「避其銳氣，擊其惰歸者」，此也。
愚也，書生，不知邊計，竊以為東南之憂不在交趾，而在猺獞諸夷；西北之憂不在哈密，而在甘肅諸鎮。其要惟在乎用人而已矣。邇者岑猛倡亂，雖就甫寧，而兩江八寨相繼煽動，府江、平樂民不安堵，驚疑莫測，有不可勝言者。誠得人如先朝所用鄧廷瓚、劉大夏者，使之經畧兩廣，庶可以紓我
translation_en:
…to isolate their forces. This is what is meant by the saying, “Acting before others can rob them of their resolve.” Alternatively, close the passes and suspend tribute, expose the deceit in their foreign-language documents, and turn back their attempts to entice people into surrender [?], thereby thwarting their schemes. Moreover, they depend entirely on us for medicines and agricultural implements. If we cut off these supplies, in time they will find themselves impoverished and hard pressed, and will repent their wrongdoing. This is what is meant by the saying, “Make others come to you, rather than being made to go to them.” Alternatively, secure the borders and give the people respite. If they come raiding, they must pass Jiaohe before reaching Jiayu, and Jiayu before reaching Gua and Sha. Carrying provisions over a thousand li, their troops will be worn out and their horses exhausted. We should strengthen our forts, guard our watchposts, gather in our livestock [?], fortify our defenses, and clear the countryside of supplies, waiting until they grow slack before striking. Unless they flee by night, they will certainly beg to surrender. This is what is meant by the saying, “Avoid their keen fighting spirit; strike them when they are sluggish and returning home.”
I am an ignorant scholar, unfamiliar with frontier strategy. Yet I venture to think that the danger in the southeast lies not in Jiaozhi but among the Yao, Zhuang, and other non-Han peoples; the danger in the northwest lies not in Hami but in the garrisons of Gansu. The essential matter is simply the employment of the right men. Recently Cen Meng fomented rebellion. Although order had only just been restored [?], the Liangjiang and Bazhai areas successively rose in unrest. The people of Fujiang and Pingle cannot live in peace; their fear and uncertainty are beyond reckoning, and the troubles are too numerous to recount. If we could truly obtain men like Deng Tingzan and Liu Daxia, whom the former reign employed, and put them in charge of administering and securing Guangdong and Guangxi, we might thereby alleviate our…

title: 嘉靖八年會試錄
text:
皇上東南之憂矣且速檀滿速兒包藏禍心牙
木蘭乃其黨類今既撫徙江統郭欽之論
可慮也况亦不剌幹爾禿厮潜居海西延
蔓滋甚肘腋之患未除而腹心之蠹猶甚
西戎北虜相為掎角有不可勝言者誠得
人如
先朝所用余子俊馬文升者使之經畧三邊庶
可以紓我
皇上西北之憂矣愚又聞之釋近謀遠者勞而
===
無功釋遠謀近者佚而有終朱熹亦曰其
備不在邊境而在
朝廷其具不在兵食而在紀綱其本不在威
强而在德業禹之無怠無荒武王之無競
惟烈商高宗之不僭不濫周宣王之矢其
文德又在
聖明留意焉
第五問
王學益

punctuated:
皇上東南之憂矣。且速檀滿速兒包藏禍心，牙木蘭乃其黨類，今既撫徙，江統、郭欽之論可慮也。况亦不剌、幹爾禿厮潜居海西，延蔓滋甚，肘腋之患未除，而腹心之蠹猶甚。西戎北虜相為掎角，有不可勝言者。誠得人如先朝所用余子俊、馬文升者，使之經畧三邊，庶可以紓我皇上西北之憂矣。愚又聞之：釋近謀遠者勞而無功，釋遠謀近者佚而有終。朱熹亦曰：「其備不在邊境而在朝廷，其具不在兵食而在紀綱，其本不在威强而在德業。」禹之無怠無荒，武王之無競惟烈，商高宗之不僭不濫，周宣王之矢其文德，又在聖明留意焉。
第五問
王學益
translation_en:
…Your Majesty’s anxieties concerning the southeast could be relieved. Moreover, Sultan Mansu’er harbors malicious designs, and Yamulan belongs to his faction. Now that they have been pacified and resettled, the arguments of Jiang Tong and Guo Qin warrant serious consideration. Furthermore, Yibula and Gan’ertusi remain concealed in Haixi, their influence spreading ever further. The danger close at hand has not been eliminated, while the forces eating away at our very heart are still more serious. The western Rong and northern barbarians support one another from opposing positions; the resulting troubles are beyond enumeration. If men like Yu Zijun and Ma Wensheng, whom former reigns employed, could indeed be found and charged with managing the Three Frontiers, we might thereby relieve Your Majesty’s anxieties concerning the northwest.
I have also heard that those who neglect what is near to devise plans for what is distant toil without success, whereas those who set aside what is distant to attend to what is near work with ease and bring matters to completion. Zhu Xi likewise said: “Defensive preparedness lies not at the frontier but at the imperial court; its means lie not in troops and provisions but in governing discipline; its foundation lies not in coercive strength but in virtuous accomplishments.” Yu’s freedom from negligence and heedlessness, King Wu’s unrivaled achievements, Shang Gaozong’s avoidance of improper rewards and excessive punishments, and King Xuan of Zhou’s display of civil virtue are likewise matters for Your enlightened Majesty’s attention.
Fifth Question
Wang Xueyi

text:
同考試官主事黃批看破古人勢變自有處
同考試官編修張批幾權妙用盡於此
考試官學士霍批亦有見
考試官大學士張批策不專言幾權而意自見
執事以成治之幾通變之權下問承學然
而愚也非知幾達權者也嘗觀宋臣蘇軾
有言漢之治凡六變其識幾者乎周敦頤
曰天下勢而已矣其達權者乎嗟乎世運
相推而變生焉盛衰相麗而幾形焉揚之
===
抑之輕之重之而權行焉有天下者不可
忽也蘇軾善言漢矣愚試比宋論之可乎
是故漢祖開基大封同姓懲孤立而弱也
未幾則侯王逆節為漢患矣是故賈誼憂
之七國平矣天下無事矣未幾而政移外
戚是故劉向憂之使誼之說見納於文帝
可無七國之變向之說見納於成帝則漢
鼎豈遽為莽染指也此幾之不察也何權
之有光武懲前代積弊不任三公不任外

translation_en:
Associate Examiner Huang, Secretary, comments: “He sees through the changing circumstances faced by men of old; this has merit of its own.”
Associate Examiner Zhang, Compiler, comments: “The subtle application of discernment and expedient judgment is fully expressed here.”
Examiner Huo, Academician, comments: “This too shows insight.”
Examiner Zhang, Grand Secretary, comments: “The policy essay does not speak exclusively of discernment and expedient judgment, yet its meaning emerges naturally.”
You, honored examiners, have condescended to question a student about discerning the incipient developments through which good government is achieved and exercising the expedient judgment through which one adapts to change. Yet I, in my ignorance, am no master of either discernment or expedient judgment. I have read the statement of Su Shi, a minister of the Song, that government under the Han underwent six transformations in all. Was he one who understood incipient developments? Zhou Dunyi said: “All under Heaven is merely a matter of the tendency of circumstances.” Was he one who understood expedient judgment? Alas! As successive ages impel one another onward, change arises; as flourishing and decline attend one another, incipient developments take shape. By promoting or restraining, giving less or greater weight, expedient judgment is exercised. Those who rule all under Heaven must not neglect this. Su Shi discussed the Han well. May I venture to discuss it by comparison with the Song?
Thus, when the founder of the Han established his dynasty, he extensively enfeoffed members of his own surname, taking warning from the weakness that comes of isolation. Before long, however, the marquises and kings rebelled and became a threat to the Han. Hence Jia Yi’s concern. The Seven Kingdoms were pacified, and all under Heaven was at peace; before long, however, political power shifted to the imperial relatives by marriage. Hence Liu Xiang’s concern. Had Emperor Wen accepted Jia Yi’s proposals, the rebellion of the Seven Kingdoms might have been avoided. Had Emperor Cheng accepted Liu Xiang’s proposals, how could Wang Mang so soon have laid his hands upon the dynastic tripod of the Han? This was a failure to discern incipient developments: what expedient judgment was there? Guangwu, taking warning from the accumulated abuses of the preceding era, did not entrust authority to the Three Dukes, nor to the imperial relatives by marriage…

title: 嘉靖八年會試錄
text:
戚自謂天下之變吾慮之已周積世之弊
吾防之已密矣曽不三傳而柄落內宦斯
時也天下所共慮者內宦而已未幾則內
宦去而漢亦不可為然則天下之變可勝
防乎考之西漢牝晨之釁始吕終王極矣
世儒且曲黨之載觀東漢內臣之勢自和
迄靈極矣朝臣復呶激之豈漢之君臣始
也不知所審尚終也不知所損益致然乎
因時觀變酌幾用權者所宜知也宋祖初
===
興鑒前代之失由是屏外戚抑宦官削武
將獨用儒學以文太平然醜虜壓境儒者
拱揖不能却敵則失之積弱熈豐以議法
啓爭元祐以三黨自釁國是士習則失之
不靖使仁宗嗣位文武並用則宋治宜振
三黨不自創殘豈有紹聖之紛紛也亦幾
之不察也何權之有盖宋自幽州之敗北
虜已横再為城下之盟則中國幾殆矣舉
朝臣子乃以納幣為常職乞和為得策恬

戚，自謂天下之變，吾慮之已周；積世之弊，吾防之已密矣。曽不三傳，而柄落內宦。斯時也，天下所共慮者，內宦而已。未幾，則內宦去，而漢亦不可為。然則天下之變，可勝防乎？考之西漢，牝晨之釁，始吕終王，極矣，世儒且曲黨之；載觀東漢，內臣之勢，自和迄靈，極矣，朝臣復呶激之。豈漢之君臣始也不知所審尚，終也不知所損益，致然乎？因時觀變、酌幾用權者所宜知也。
宋祖初興，鑒前代之失，由是屏外戚，抑宦官，削武將，獨用儒學以文太平。然醜虜壓境，儒者拱揖，不能却敵，則失之積弱；熈豐以議法啓爭，元祐以三黨自釁，國是士習，則失之不靖。使仁宗嗣位，文武並用，則宋治宜振；三黨不自創殘，豈有紹聖之紛紛也？亦幾之不察也，何權之有？盖宋自幽州之敗，北虜已横，再為城下之盟，則中國幾殆矣。舉朝臣子乃以納幣為常職，乞和為得策，恬
translation_en:
…imperial relatives by marriage, thinking to himself: “I have considered every possible upheaval in the realm, and my safeguards against the abuses accumulated over generations are already thorough.” Yet before even three successions had passed, power fell into the hands of palace eunuchs. At that time, the eunuchs alone were the common concern of all under Heaven. Before long, the eunuchs were removed, but the Han could no longer be saved either. Can every upheaval in the realm, then, possibly be guarded against? Examining the Western Han, we find that the calamity of hens crowing at dawn—women usurping authority—began with Lü and ended with Wang, reaching its utmost extent; yet scholars of the age perversely took their side. Looking also at the Eastern Han, we find that the power of palace eunuchs, from Emperor He through Emperor Ling, reached its utmost extent; yet court officials further inflamed it with their clamorous attacks. Did this result because the Han rulers and ministers initially failed to discern what they should esteem, and ultimately failed to understand what they should curtail or augment? Those who observe changes in accordance with the times and weigh incipient developments in exercising discretionary judgment ought to understand this.
When the founding emperor of the Song first rose to power, he took warning from the failures of preceding dynasties. Accordingly, he excluded imperial relatives by marriage, restrained eunuchs, curtailed military commanders, and employed Confucian learning alone to embellish an age of peace. But when the vile northern foes pressed upon the borders, the Confucian scholars could only bow with hands clasped, unable to repel the enemy: here the failing was cumulative weakness. During the Xining and Yuanfeng eras, debate over new laws provoked contention; during the Yuanyou era, the three factions brought strife upon themselves. In national policy and the habits of scholars, the failing was a lack of tranquility. Had Emperor Renzong, upon succeeding to the throne, employed civil and military talents together, Song governance should have flourished. Had the three factions not wounded and destroyed one another, how could the turmoil of the Shaosheng era have arisen? This too was a failure to discern incipient developments. What exercise of discretionary judgment was there? Since the Song defeat at Youzhou, the northern foes had already grown overbearing; when a further covenant was made beneath the city walls, the realm was nearly imperiled. Yet the ministers and servants of the entire court treated the delivery of tribute as a routine duty and begging for peace as sound policy, complacently…

title: 嘉靖八年會試錄
text:
且安焉靖康之及識者占諸獻納之議可
知也抑宋祖以詐得國故多防詐然猜防
既多則臣下有不得盡忠者矣復以點檢
即祚故忌武臣然武畧絀屈則中國積衰
矣豈宋之君臣始也審尚已偏終也因循
愈弊致然乎亦因時觀變酌幾用權者所
宜知也嗟夫創業之君之自貽哲命也造
化主宰自我者也是故造命之道貴于謹
審守成之君之祈天永命也造化轉移自
===
我者也是故永命之道貴乎敬慎漢宋君
臣不足與於斯也洪惟我
太祖皇帝以三十餘年定治體
太宗皇帝以二十餘年弘治化制度紀綱盡美
盡善更僕未易竟也語其大者如
藩封星列天下鞏磐石之宗蓋鑒宋藩之聚
居而致悔祿糧歲供昪翰無專地之患則
鑒漢封之過制而難馭為法之善上兼虞
周賈誼之憂今所無也

鑒漢封之過制而難馭為法之善上兼虞
周貫誼之憂今所無也
punctuated:
且安焉。靖康之及，識者占諸獻納之議，可知也。抑宋祖以詐得國，故多防詐；然猜防既多，則臣下有不得盡忠者矣。復以點檢即祚，故忌武臣；然武畧絀屈，則中國積衰矣。豈宋之君臣始也審尚已偏，終也因循愈弊致然乎？亦因時觀變、酌幾用權者所宜知也。嗟夫！創業之君之自貽哲命也，造化主宰自我者也，是故造命之道貴于謹審；守成之君之祈天永命也，造化轉移自我者也，是故永命之道貴乎敬慎。漢宋君臣不足與於斯也。
洪惟我太祖皇帝以三十餘年定治體，太宗皇帝以二十餘年弘治化，制度紀綱盡美盡善，更僕未易竟也。語其大者，如藩封星列天下，鞏磐石之宗，蓋鑒宋藩之聚居而致悔；祿糧歲供，昪翰無專地之患，則鑒漢封之過制而難馭。為法之善，上兼虞周，賈誼之憂，今所無也。
translation_en:
…and were content with it. That the calamity of Jingkang would befall them could already be foreseen by discerning men from the deliberations over presenting tribute. Moreover, the founding emperor of the Song obtained the realm through deception and therefore took many precautions against deception. Yet, with suspicion and precautions so pervasive, some of his subjects could not fully discharge their loyalty. Again, because he ascended the throne from the post of Commander-in-Chief of the Palace Command, he distrusted military officials. Yet, when military strategy was curtailed, the Central Realm grew progressively weaker. Could this have resulted from the Song rulers and ministers having biased preferences [?] at the outset, and then allowing abuses to worsen through habitual inaction? This, too, should be understood by those who observe changes as circumstances unfold, weigh incipient developments, and exercise discretion.
Alas! When a founding ruler secures for himself a wisely ordained mandate, mastery of the processes of creation and transformation lies in himself. Thus, the way to establish the mandate values care and deliberation. When a ruler preserving an established dynasty prays to Heaven for an enduring mandate, the power to redirect those processes lies in himself. Thus, the way to perpetuate the mandate values reverence and caution. The rulers and ministers of the Han and Song fall short of this.
We reverently reflect that our Emperor Taizu spent more than thirty years establishing the structure of government, and Emperor Taizong spent more than twenty years extending its civilizing influence. Their institutions, regulations, and governing principles were perfect in every respect; even with successive attendants taking their turns, an account of them could scarcely be finished. To speak of the greater matters: the princely fiefs are scattered like stars throughout the realm, securing the imperial lineage as firmly as a great rock. This surely reflects the lesson of the Song princes, whose residence together brought cause for regret. Stipends in grain are supplied annually, and the princes serving as the dynasty’s supports [?] present no danger of exercising exclusive control over territory. This reflects the lesson of the Han enfeoffments, which exceeded proper limits and became difficult to control. In the excellence of its institutions, our dynasty combines the achievements of ancient Yu and Zhou. The dangers that troubled Jia Yi do not exist today.

title: 嘉靖八年會試錄
text:
宮闈之令不出房闥則高曹向孟不足稱賢
戚畹之貴不與政事則祿産鳳莽不能為
孽防慮之周下鑒歷代劉向之憂亦今所
無也内臣職典監局自有定貟且嚴交結
之禁武臣位秩特列文臣之右預防絀武
之弊則東漢宦官之釁前宋武備之衰今
皆無之治體畫一萬世可守不必如西漢
之更化四夷率服中國尊安無復如宋人
之積弱是皆
===
皇祖審尚極正故無後弊可虞
太宗持守極善故無損益可議乃今竊聞
藩封日盛祿糧不繼而
宗室屢困武職日冗俸給不充而材勇愈乏
文臣玩愒職守弗虔武臣頑懦邊防弛敝
北方則田野多蕪南嶠則寇竊時警蘇浙
則賦斂日急而民愈困甘涼則羌戎歲擾
而兵愈疲是皆因循漸積之弊非
皇祖制治意也仰惟

皇祖制治意也仰惟
punctuated:
宮闈之令不出房闥，則高曹向孟不足稱賢；戚畹之貴不與政事，則祿産鳳莽不能為孽。防慮之周，下鑒歷代，劉向之憂亦今所無也。内臣職典監局，自有定貟，且嚴交結之禁；武臣位秩特列文臣之右，預防絀武之弊，則東漢宦官之釁、前宋武備之衰，今皆無之。治體畫一，萬世可守，不必如西漢之更化；四夷率服，中國尊安，無復如宋人之積弱。是皆皇祖審尚極正，故無後弊可虞；太宗持守極善，故無損益可議。
乃今竊聞，藩封日盛，祿糧不繼，而宗室屢困；武職日冗，俸給不充，而材勇愈乏。文臣玩愒，職守弗虔；武臣頑懦，邊防弛敝。北方則田野多蕪，南嶠則寇竊時警，蘇浙則賦斂日急而民愈困，甘涼則羌戎歲擾而兵愈疲。是皆因循漸積之弊，非皇祖制治意也。仰惟
translation_en:
Commands from the inner palace do not pass beyond its doors; thus Gao, Cao, Xiang, and Meng need not be singled out as paragons of virtue. Noble imperial relatives by marriage take no part in government affairs; thus men such as Lü Lu, Lü Chan, Wang Feng, and Wang Mang cannot work mischief. So comprehensive are these precautions, drawing lessons from successive dynasties, that the dangers Liu Xiang feared likewise do not exist today. The eunuchs administer the directorates and bureaus, with fixed staffing complements and strict prohibitions against forming outside connections. Military officials are expressly ranked above civil officials, forestalling the harm of slighting military affairs. Thus neither the troubles caused by eunuchs in the Eastern Han nor the decline of military preparedness under the former Song exists today. The framework of government is uniform and can be maintained for ten thousand generations, without any need for a change of course such as occurred under the Western Han. The foreign peoples of the four quarters all submit, and the Central Kingdom enjoys honor and security, free from the accumulated weakness of the Song. All this is because the imperial ancestor’s considered priorities were entirely correct [?], leaving no subsequent abuses to fear, and because Taizong maintained these institutions with consummate skill, leaving no additions or reductions to debate.
Yet now I have privately heard that princely establishments increase daily, while grain stipends fail to keep pace, repeatedly leaving members of the imperial clan in straitened circumstances. Military posts grow ever more redundant, while salaries are insufficient and capable, courageous men become increasingly scarce. Civil officials idle away their time and neglect their duties; military officials are obtuse and cowardly, and frontier defenses have become lax and dilapidated. In the north, much farmland lies waste; in the southern mountains, banditry repeatedly causes alarm. In Suzhou and Zhejiang, the exaction of taxes grows more pressing by the day and the people become increasingly impoverished; in Ganzhou and Liangzhou, the Qiang and Rong cause disturbances every year and the troops become increasingly exhausted. These are all abuses that have gradually accumulated through complacent adherence to routine; they were not the imperial ancestor’s intention in establishing the government. Reverently I reflect…

punctuated: 聖人在上，天德純健，離照貞明，酌幾審權，懋隆治化，諒自有道。執事佑賛密勿，嘉猷入告可也。草莽衣褐之言，又奚辱聽焉？
translation_en: …the sage sovereign reigns above, his heavenly virtue pure and vigorous, his illuminating discernment steadfast and bright. He weighs the subtle beginnings of affairs and carefully considers expedient measures; surely he has his own way to foster flourishing government and moral transformation. You, honored officials, may assist him with diligent devotion and present sound counsel to the throne. Why, then, should you deign to hear the words of a rustic clad in coarse cloth?

translation_en:
Postface to the Record of the Metropolitan Examination

For the Metropolitan Examination of the eighth year [of Jiajing, 1529], His Majesty commanded us, his servants Cong and Tao, to preside over the examination. After entering the examination compound, your servant Cong summoned the assembled functionaries and addressed them: “This undertaking is to seek truly worthy men for our sage Son of Heaven. Should we not exercise care? Are there candidates who bring in concealed writings, hoping to succeed by luck? Are there those who gather in groups of five or ten, plagiarizing arguments and repeating one another’s words without scruple? Expel them to punish their disregard for the rules. Are there cases in which the sealing of identifying information is confused, allowing disclosure, bribery, or assistance [?]? Are there copyists who work carelessly, omitting material or making errors? Should we not guard against these things so that no talent is overlooked? All you functionaries outside the curtain, exercise care!” He further said: “When learning is unsound, the disposition of the mind becomes crooked. If candidates plagiarize and rehearse Zhuangzi, Laozi, the various philosophical masters, or unofficial histories to parade their erudition and display curiosities, set their papers aside without reading them. As for the changed forms of the Odes …

translation_en: …and those passages of the Rites that are intricate and minute contain the supreme Way; use these especially to examine candidates. As for grouping events from the Spring and Autumn Annals for comparison, thereby fragmenting the sage’s classic, follow Master Zhu’s authoritative injunction and do not use this to examine candidates. Should not all of us serving within the examination curtain be vigilant in these matters?” At the time, I, your servant, said nothing. Once the candidates had been selected, a record was compiled for presentation to the throne. I then declared: “Do all of us charged with these duties know how to serve our sovereign? Worthy and talented men belong to the altars of soil and grain—the state. His Majesty seeks talent for the state. If we, his servants, greedily claim this as our own achievement, what greater offense against the state could there be? 敢曰：「士由吾進，為吾門生」，市私恩乎？又曰：「爾多士進矣，服事庶僚，鞠躬誓心，下衞生民，上衞社稷，圖報聖天子，為帝室公臣。無德舉主，偪曲阿比，以獲戾社稷。是爾乃社稷之臣也。其慎諸！於戲，其尚慎諸！」
通議大夫、詹事府詹事兼翰林院學士霍韜謹序。
translation_en:
…dare say, “These scholars advanced through me and are my disciples,” thereby buying their personal gratitude? He further said: “You scholars have now advanced. Serving in the various offices, bow yourselves in devotion and pledge your hearts; below, protect the people, and above, protect the altars of soil and grain. Seek to repay the sagely Son of Heaven and serve the imperial house in the public interest. Do not regard your examiners as personal benefactors and engage in constrained compliance, flattery, and factional attachment [?], thereby offending against the altars of soil and grain. Thus you will indeed be servants of the state. Be watchful! Ah, may you remain watchful!”
Respectfully prefaced by Huo Tao, Grand Master for Thorough Counsel, Household Administrator of the Heir Apparent, and concurrently Academician of the Hanlin Academy.
